1.pericope_label: What advantage then hath the Jew? or what profit is there of circumcision? Much every way: chiefly, because that unto them were committed the oracles of God

schools.summary: Gill asks where the superior excellency of the Jew lies if a Jew is not properly one born of Jewish parents and brought up in the customs and religion of the nation, but anyone of whatever nation who is born again of water and of the Spirit, since on that footing a man may as well be born and brought up a Heathen as a Jew. He renders the phrase as what hath the Jew more, or what has he superfluous or abundant, and traces it to the Hebrew idiom rendered elsewhere what profit hath a man, what hath a wise man more, and what is a man better, noting how the Septuagint turns those passages. The answer he glosses from the Rabbinic phrases for in all respects and on every side. Calvin explains why the objection had to be removed at all: Paul had proved that bare circumcision brought nothing to the Jews, yet he could not deny that there was some difference between Gentile and Jew which that symbol sealed to them from the Lord, and it was inconsistent to make void a distinction of which God was the author; the glorying was foolish, but a doubt remained as to the design of circumcision, since the Lord would not have appointed it had no benefit been intended, and it was a partition-wall which kept the parties asunder. In the answer he begins to give the sacrament its own praise without conceding the pride, since the Jews were sealed by the symbol of circumcision and counted the children of God not through any merit or worthiness of their own but through the free mercy of God; regarded as men they were on a level with others, but if the favours of God be taken into the account they possessed what made them more eminent. The word rendered chiefly he denies to be a note of number, taking it for especially and citing three other places where it bears that sense, though he records that some think the period unfinished; the sense is that though it were but this one thing, that the oracles of God were committed to them, it might be deemed sufficient to prove their superiority. He insists that the advantage of circumcision is not made to consist in the naked sign but that its value is derived from the word, since Paul asks what benefit the sacrament conferred and answers that God had deposited with them the treasure of celestial wisdom, from which it follows that apart from the word no excellency remained. By the oracles he understands the covenant revealed first to Abraham and his posterity and afterwards sealed and unfolded by the law and the prophets, committed to them that they might preserve them as long as it pleased the Lord to continue his glory among them and then publish them through the whole world, so that they were first depositories and secondly dispensers; and he closes by turning the benefit into a reproach, that if it was so highly to be esteemed when one nation only was favoured with the revelation of the word, we can never sufficiently reprobate our own ingratitude in receiving it with so much negligence or carelessness, not to say disdain.

Henry treats the opening as the first of a series of objections which the apostle answers to clear his way, since no truth is so plain but wicked wits and corrupt carnal hearts will have something to say against it. The objection is that God has often spoken with great respect for the Jews as a people like no other, a holy nation, a peculiar treasure, the seed of Abraham his friend, and instituted circumcision as a badge of church-membership and a seal of covenant relation, so that a levelling doctrine seems to deny them all such prerogatives and to reflect dishonour upon the ordinance as a fruitless insignificant thing. The answer is that they are notwithstanding a people greatly privileged and honoured, with great means and helps, though these are not infallibly saving: the door is open to the Gentiles as well as the Jews, but the Jews have a fairer way up to this door by reason of their church-privileges, which are not to be undervalued though many that have them perish eternally for not improving them. Of the many privileges he reckons up elsewhere he mentions here but one, which he calls equivalent to all, that the oracles of God were committed to them, that is the scriptures of the Old Testament, especially the law of Moses, and those types, promises and prophecies which relate to Christ and the gospel. The scriptures are the oracles of God, a divine revelation, come from heaven, of infallible truth and of eternal consequence; the Septuagint calls the Urim and Thummim the oracles, and the scripture is our breast-plate of judgment, to which we must have recourse as to an oracle. These were committed to the Jews as trustees for succeeding ages and churches, the Old Testament being written in their language and deposited in their hands to be carefully preserved pure and uncorrupt and transmitted to posterity; they were the Christians’ library-keepers, entrusted with that sacred treasure for their own benefit first and then for the advantage of the world, and in preserving the letter of the scripture they were very faithful to their trust and did not lose one iota or tittle, in which we are to acknowledge God’s gracious care and providence. They had the means of salvation, he adds, but they had not the monopoly of salvation; and the enjoyment of God’s word and ordinances is the chief happiness of a people, to be put first among their advantages.

Clarke summarises the chapter as pointing out the peculiar privileges of the Jews and then showing that they too had sinned and forfeited all right and title to God’s especial favour. He quotes Dr Taylor at length: in the preceding chapter the apostle has carried his argument to the utmost length, and what remains is to keep the Jew in temper, to fix his convictions and to draw the grand conclusion; having shown that the Jews were more wicked than the Gentiles and that law, circumcision and outward profession were no ground of acceptance, he had in effect said that they had forfeited their right to the privileges of God’s peculiar people and stood in need of a fresh display of grace, which if they rejected God would cast them out of the vineyard. The apostle was sensible that the Jew would understand him so and that it must be very irritating to hear that his law, circumcision and external advantages were utterly insufficient to procure the favour of God, and therefore, knowing what his countrymen would be ready to say, he introduces a dialogue between himself and a Jew in which he gives him leave to answer and defend himself. On that view Clarke prefixes the speakers to the questions and answers of the first nine verses to make the whole more intelligible, giving the Jew the opening question: you lately allowed that circumcision verily profited, but if our being in covenant with God raises us no higher in the divine favour than the Gentiles, and if the virtuous among them are as acceptable as any of us and condemn our nation too, tell me wherein lies the superior honour of the Jew. The answer he gives to the Apostle: the Jews, in reference to the means and motives of obedience, enjoy many advantages beyond the Gentiles, and principally because to them were committed the oracles of God, that revelation of his will to Moses and the prophets which contains a treasure of excellencies with which no other part of the world has been favoured, though they have most grievously abused these privileges. Wesley glosses the circumcision as meaning those that are circumcised, and takes the oracles for the scriptures, in which are so great and precious promises; other prerogatives, he notes, will follow later in the epistle, and Paul here singles out this one by which, after removing the objection, he will convict them so much the more.

Barnes explains that the design of the first part of the chapter is to answer objections which might be offered by a Jew to the statements of the last, the first of them being stated in this verse: a Jew would naturally ask what peculiar benefit he could derive from his religion, the objection arising particularly from the position that if a heathen should do the things required by the law he would be treated as if he had been circumcised. The answer he renders as in every respect, and takes the privilege named as the principal one and the one including all others, the main benefit of being a Jew being to possess the sacred Scriptures and their instructions. The word translated committed he identifies as the one commonly employed to express faith or confidence, implying confidence on the part of God in entrusting his oracles to them, a confidence not misplaced, since no people ever guarded a sacred trust with more fidelity than the Jews did the Scriptures. Oracle among the heathen meant properly the answer or response of a god, or of some priest supposed to be inspired, to an inquiry of importance, usually expressed in a brief sententious way and often with great ambiguity, and the place from which such a response was obtained was also called an oracle, as at Delphi; the word occurs in the New Testament but four times, and is used here to denote the Scriptures as being that which was spoken by God, and particularly perhaps the divine promises. No higher favour, he adds, can be conferred on a people, which should excite our gratitude and lead us to endeavour to extend them to other nations. Ellicott glosses chiefly as in the first place, observing that a secondly was to follow but does not, the Apostle being drawn away to other topics; he calls the English rendering of the next clause paraphrastic, since oracle is the object and not the subject of the sentence and the sense is that they were entrusted with them, and he judges oracles a good translation for the Scriptures of the Old Testament as containing a revelation of God. Robertson renders the question literally as what then is the overplus of the Jew, what the Jew has over and above the Gentile, and calls it a pertinent question after the stinging indictment of the previous chapter; the noun for profit he glosses as the help, an old word occurring only here in the New Testament. In the answer he takes the adjective as pointing back to the overplus, so that it is much from every angle, and notes that as elsewhere Paul does not add to his first but singles out one privilege of the many possessed by the Jew. The verb he parses as a first aorist passive with the accusative of the thing retained, and the noun for oracles as probably a diminutive of the word for word, early used of the responses from Delphi and common in the Greek Old Testament for the oracles of the Lord, though from Philo onward used of any sacred writing including narrative; it is possible, he allows, that the idea here includes all the Old Testament.

Theodoret states the objection in its own terms: if some among heathen and alien nations who were adorned with piety and virtue share in the divine favour, to what good did God separate Israel from the Gentiles and give them the rite of circumcision, since by the more of the Jew he means advantage above the Gentiles. The answer he expands into a history: God chose their ancestors, freed them from the dominion of the Egyptians, made them the wonder of nations by miracles of all kinds, gave the law for their assistance and set over them his prophets, and this is what is meant by much in every way; yet omitting the specific enumeration of all these he is content to mention the institution of the law alone, since this was the highest honour, that while the other nations possessed only the knowledge which nature gives, they had received the gift of the law in addition.

debates: Whether an enumeration is begun and left unfinished: Ellicott holds that a secondly was to follow and never comes, the Apostle being drawn away to other topics, and records that some read an unfinished period; Calvin denies that the word is a note of number at all and takes it for especially, citing three parallels; Wesley says the further prerogatives do come, later in the epistle.

What the advantage actually consists in: Calvin insists it lies not in the naked sign but in the word attached to it, so that apart from the word no excellency remained; Theodoret rehearses the whole national history, the calling of the fathers, the exodus, the miracles and the prophets, before reducing it to the law; Henry allows the Jews the means of salvation but not the monopoly of it.

How the trust was kept: Barnes says the divine confidence was not misplaced, no people ever having guarded a sacred deposit more faithfully, and Henry that they did not lose one iota or tittle of the letter; Clarke grants the treasure but adds that they most grievously abused the privilege.
outliers: Clarke stages the opening nine verses as a formal dialogue and prefixes the speakers to each question and answer, on Dr Taylor’s view that Paul gives his countryman leave to defend himself.
Gill traces the opening phrase to a Hebrew idiom rendered elsewhere as what profit hath a man and what is a man better, and notes how the Septuagint turns those passages.
Barnes digresses into the heathen use of the word oracle, the brief and often ambiguous response of a god or inspired priest, and the seat of such responses at Delphi.
Calvin turns the privilege into a reproach of his own readers, who receive the same word with negligence and carelessness, not to say disdain.

3.pericope_label: For what if some did not believe? shall their unbelief make the faith of God without effect? God forbid: yea, let God be true, but every man a liar; as it is written, That thou mightest be justified in thy sayings, and mightest overcome when thou art judged

schools.summary: Gill takes the unbelief as an aggravation of their sin, that men with such means of light and knowledge and such clear evidences should be incredulous, but insists it was the case only of some and not of all, and that it must be understood not of disbelieving the Scriptures to be the word of God, since these were always received as such by them all and were constantly read and heard and attended to, but either of disobedience to the commands of God required in the law, or of disregard to the promises of God and the prophecies of the Messiah, and of disbelief in the Messiah himself when he came; this was therefore no objection to their advantage over the Gentiles, since it was owing not to any want of evidence in the word of God but to the darkness and unbelief of their own minds. The answer he takes as a rule never to be given up, that the truth of God cannot be made of none effect by the want of faith in man, God being faithful to his word, constant in his promises and certain to fulfil his purposes, though every man is vain, fallacious and inconstant. Calvin explains that having allowed the Jews no spark of glory while they exulted in the naked sign, Paul now considers the nature of the sign and testifies that its virtue is not destroyed even by their inconstancy; anticipating the objection that whatever grace there was in circumcision had wholly vanished through their ingratitude, he asks again what opinion was to be formed of it. He hears a deliberate reticence in the word some, since Paul might truly have said that a great part of the nation had renounced the covenant of God, but as this would have been very grating to Jewish ears he mitigated its severity. The verb he glosses as properly meaning to render void and ineffectual, and defines the question precisely: not so much whether the unbelief of men neutralises the truth of God so that it should not remain firm in itself, but whether it hinders its effect and fulfilment as to men; and the answer is that the truth of God cannot lose its stability through man’s wickedness, so that though the greater part trod the covenant under foot it yet retained its efficacy and manifested its power, not as to all but with regard to a few of that nation, some ever remaining who by continuing to believe the promise had not fallen away from the privileges of the covenant, since the covenant is confirmed on both sides only when the promise is received by faith. In the following verse he finds an argument taken from the necessary consequence of what is opposed to it: since the two propositions stand together and necessarily accord, that God is true and that man is false, the truth of God is not nullified by the falsehood of men but thereby becomes more evident. God is true, he says, not only because he is prepared to stand faithfully to his promises but because he really fulfils whatever he declares, so speaking that his command becomes a reality; man is false not only because he often violates his pledged faith but because he naturally seeks falsehood and shuns the truth. The first clause he calls the primary axiom of all Christian philosophy and the second a quotation from the Psalms, where David confesses that there is nothing certain from man or in man; and he calls the passage a remarkable one containing a much needed consolation, since such is the perversity of men in despising God’s word that its truth would often be doubted did we not remember that God’s verity depends not on man’s. To the difficulty that faith is nevertheless required on the part of men if the promise is to be effectual, he answers that the Lord, notwithstanding the lies of men, finds a way for his truth through a pathless track by correcting in his elect the inbred unbelief of our nature and subjecting to his service those who seem unconquerable, the discourse here being concerned with the corruption of nature and not with the grace which remedies it. Of the quotation he says that by the sayings of God David means the judgments God pronounces upon us, the common application of them to promises being too strained, and that the particle implies an inference rather than a far-fetched consequence: against thee have I sinned, justly then dost thou punish me. He holds that Paul quotes according to the real meaning of David, since otherwise the objection immediately following would have been raised in vain; that the second Hebrew clause imports that God in all his judgments is worthy of praise however the ungodly clamour; and that although the Greek verb may be taken actively as well as passively, the Greek translators rendered it passively contrary to the meaning of the Prophet, Paul following the Greek version because it answered his purpose here even better, the Apostles in quoting Scripture often using freer language than the original and counting it enough to quote what was suitable to their subject.

Clarke continues his dialogue and assigns the question to the Jew: if some of the Jewish nation have abused their privileges and acted contrary to their obligations, shall their wickedness annul the promise God made to Abraham that he would by an everlasting covenant be a God to him and to his seed after him, and shall God, by stripping the Jews of their peculiar honour, falsify his promise to the nation because some of the Jews are bad men? The Apostle’s answer he renders as let it not be, far from it, by no means: we must ever maintain that God is true, and that if in any case his promise appear to fail it is because the condition on which it was given has not been complied with. This he takes to be the sense of the psalm, reading it through the history: David acknowledges his sin and condemns himself, that the truth of the promise to establish his house and throne for ever may be vindicated when God executes the dreadful threatening that the sword shall never depart from his house, which he owns he has brought upon himself by his own iniquity. Should any man say that the promise of God had failed toward him, Clarke concludes, let him examine his heart and his ways and he will find that he has departed out of that way in which alone God could, consistently with his holiness and truth, fulfil the promise. Wesley answers the objection in a single clause, asking whether God will not still make good his promises to them that do believe.

Barnes treats the verse as another objection of a Jew and sets out its steps: the apostle had maintained that the nation was sinful, the objector admits this of some, and then asks whether it does not involve the inadmissible consequence that God is unfaithful, since the choice of the nation and the covenant with the fathers seemed to imply that the Jews should be kept from perdition; it was their belief that all Jews would be saved, and the doctrine of the previous chapter would put them on a level with the Gentiles, so that they ask of what value the promise was. The word for faith here he takes to mean the faithfulness or fidelity of God to his promises, and the phrase for making it of no effect to mean destroying it or preventing him from fulfilling them. The answer he renders as let not this by any means be supposed, and explains that the fidelity of God could be maintained consistently with the rejection of any number of Jews, since the promise to Abraham and the fathers was not unconditional and absolute but implied obedience, as the apostle shows at length later in the epistle. The principle that God should be esteemed true whatever consequence follows he calls a fixed position where every man might find rest, and one which would do more than all things else to allay the tempests of human life; the willingness to abandon every opinion of one’s own that impinges on the veracity of God he calls an illustration of the humility of true piety, and he adds that no man who felt it could for a moment be a Universalist, and none could be an infidel. The quotation he calls one of the most beautiful and most happy ever made, David being overwhelmed with grief and holding it as a fixed and indisputable principle that God was right, never once thinking of calling it in question; to be justified is to be regarded as just, the verb rendered overcome is sometimes used of one who gains his cause in a court of justice, and the whole is to be read as if there were a trial between David and God in which God would be esteemed pure and righteous in his sentence. Ellicott paraphrases the opening as a question of how the case stands: if some rejected the faith, shall their rejection defeat the faithfulness of God? He notes that the objection is that the Jews had forfeited and cancelled their privilege by unbelief, and that Paul first reduces it to its proper limits, since it was not all but some who were unbelievers, but that even granting some, this fact would have no power to shake the eternal promises of God. The reply he renders as, rather let God be seen to be true though all mankind should be proved false, even as the Psalmist looked upon his own sin as serving to enhance the triumph of God’s justice, speaking of that justice for the moment as if it could be arraigned before the bar of a still higher tribunal and asserting its absolute and complete acquittal. The purpose clause he renders strictly as in order that, here as in the Hebrew, and comments that good is in some way inscrutable to us educed out of evil, clearly foreseen by God and forming part of his design, though so as not to interfere with the free will of man; religion assumes that free will and omnipotence are reconcilable, though how seems an insoluble problem, and the same difficulty attaches to every system but one of blank fatalism and atheism, which if logically carried out would simply destroy human society. He notes that the psalm is commonly, though perhaps wrongly, ascribed to David after his sin with Bathsheba, the effect of the sin being to throw into the strongest relief the justice of the sentence that follows it, and that where the original reads that thou mightest be pure in thy judging, Paul adopts the rendering of the Greek version, which makes the last word passive instead of active and so applies it not to the sentence given by God but to the imaginary trial to which by a figure of speech that sentence is supposed to be submitted. Robertson notes the exclamatory use of the opening words, and parses the verb of unbelief as an old one meaning to disbelieve, which is the common New Testament meaning, adding that it also means to be unfaithful to one’s trust and that Lightfoot argues for that idea here; either makes sense and both are true of some of the Jews, especially concerning the Messianic promises and Jesus, and these were the depositaries and guardians of revelation. The noun he says undoubtedly means faithfulness here and not faith, God having been faithful whether the Jews simply disbelieved or were untrue to their trust, and though Paul can use the words in two senses in this verse there is no real objection to taking all three to refer to faithfulness. The following imperative he renders as let God continue to be true, a present middle, and the contrast as meaning though every man be found a liar; the purpose particle he notes is not the commoner one, and the verb of justification, used of God, has to mean declared righteous and not made righteous.

Theodoret answers the objection from the divine foreknowledge: the God of all knew well from of old both who would keep his law and who would break it, and therefore they who did not believe by no means invalidated the divine mercies; nay, even though all mankind should prove ungrateful towards him, this ingratitude could not diminish the glory of God. On the following clause he grants the case for argument’s sake, that no one soul of man offered him the praise and honour due but all were infected with ingratitude, which is what is meant by every man being false, and asks what diminution God’s glory would suffer from it.

debates: What the unbelief was: Robertson allows both that the verb means to disbelieve and that it means to be unfaithful to a trust, citing Lightfoot for the latter, and holds that all three related words in the verse may equally be read of faithfulness; Gill denies outright that any of them disbelieved the Scriptures to be God’s word, and confines the unbelief to disobedience and to the rejection of the Messiah.

How the passage from the Psalms should be rendered: Ellicott observes that Paul follows the Greek version, which turns the last verb passive and so refers it to an imagined trial of God’s own sentence; Calvin agrees on the fact but says the Greek was rendered contrary to the Prophet’s meaning, and that Paul used it because it answered his purpose even better.

How the promise can stand while many perish: Calvin holds that the covenant kept its efficacy in the few who continued to believe; Barnes answers that the promise was never unconditional, obedience being implied throughout; Clarke says simply that the condition on which it was given has not been complied with.
outliers: Barnes remarks that a man who genuinely held God’s veracity as a first principle could not for a moment be a Universalist, and could not be an infidel.

Ellicott turns aside to the difficulty underneath the verse, that good is drawn out of evil by design without overriding free will, granting that how freedom and omnipotence agree seems insoluble while insisting the alternative would destroy human society.
Calvin hears deliberate understatement in the word some, since Paul might truly have said that a great part of the nation had renounced the covenant but softened it for Jewish ears.
Clarke reads the psalm through the history of David’s house, the confession vindicating the promise at the very moment the threatened sword falls.

5.pericope_label: But if our unrighteousness commend the righteousness of God, what shall we say? Is God unrighteous who taketh vengeance? (I speak as a man) God forbid: for then how shall God judge the world? For if the truth of God hath more abounded through my lie unto his glory; why yet am I also judged as a sinner? And not rather, (as we be slanderously reported, and as some affirm that we say,) Let us do evil, that good may come? whose damnation is just

schools.summary: Gill holds that the unrighteousness of men commends the faithfulness of God only in the sense of manifesting and illustrating it, since all unrighteousness is sin, the wrath of God is revealed against it, and one thing cannot of its own nature influence its contrary; the righteousness of God is illustrated in punishing the unrighteousness of men, in setting forth Christ to be a propitiation for sin, and in fulfilling his promises notwithstanding the failings of his people, of which the case of David is a pregnant proof, just as the love of God is commended by the consideration of the sins of those for whom Christ died. The inference he calls detestable and abominable and refuses to allow that it can be fairly deduced, distinguishing that it is the unrighteousness of God’s own people, on whom he takes no personal vengeance, and not the unrighteousness of others, on whom he does, which commends his righteousness; and even granting the other case, God cannot be unrighteous in performing his threatenings in a way of righteousness. Unrighteousness, he repeats, does not of itself but by accident illustrate the righteousness of God, and nothing is more certain than that God will judge the world and will do it in righteousness, which could not be were he unrighteous in taking vengeance. The final slander he treats as the apostle’s own words put into the objector’s mouth, as if to say, why do you not go on, why do you stop here, and not rather say plainly what we are evil spoken of for. Calvin calls the passage a digression which was yet necessary, lest Paul should seem to give the ill-disposed an occasion to speak evil, since they were watching for every opportunity to defame the gospel and might have founded a calumny on the testimony of David: if God seeks nothing but to be glorified by men, why does he punish them when they offend, since by offending they glorify him? Lest anyone should think Paul expressed the sentiment of his own mind, he premises that he assumes the person of the ungodly, and at the same time touches human reason by a single expression, saying not according to the ungodly but according to man, for all the mysteries of God are paradoxes to the flesh, which possesses so much audacity that it fears not to oppose them and insolently to assail what it cannot comprehend; whence we are reminded that if we desire to understand them we must labour to be freed from our own reason and unreservedly to submit to his word. In checking the blasphemy Paul gives not a direct reply but begins by expressing his abhorrence, which Calvin thinks more weighty than a simple denial, since it implies that the expression deserved to be regarded with horror and not to be heard; the refutation which follows is indirect, taken from an office which belongs to God, not from his mere power but from his exercised power, which shines forth in the whole arrangement of his works, for it is God’s work to judge the world, to rectify it by his own righteousness and to reduce to the best order whatever is out of order, and he cannot then determine anything unjustly. He hears an allusion to Abraham’s plea over Sodom, that it is not meet that he who is to judge the earth should destroy the just with the ungodly, and a parallel in Job; among men unjust judges are found because they usurp authority contrary to law, or are inconsiderately raised to eminence, or degenerate from themselves, but there is nothing of this kind with God, who being by nature judge must be just, for he cannot deny himself. Though this extends to the constant government of God, Calvin allows it a special reference to the last judgment, when a real restoration of just order will take place; and he adds the direct refutation Paul withheld, that it comes not through what unrighteousness is that God’s righteousness becomes more illustrious, but that our wickedness is so surpassed by God’s goodness that it is turned to serve an end different from that to which it tends. The next objection he again ascribes to the ungodly, an explanation of the former verse which would have been connected with it had not the Apostle, moved with indignation, broken off the sentence in the middle, and he remarks how the Apostle changes his words while the same things are essentially meant, his style being throughout Hebraistic. The last clause he calls elliptical, requiring a word to be understood, and says the Apostle deigns not to answer the slander, though we may check it by the most solid reason: evil cannot of itself produce anything but evil, and that God’s glory is illustrated through our sin is not the work of man but the work of God, who as a wonderful worker knows how to overcome our wickedness and to convert it to an end contrary to what we intend. God has prescribed the way in which he would have himself glorified, even by true piety, which consists in obedience to his word, and he who leaps over this boundary strives not to honour God but to dishonour him. Calvin closes by observing that there has never been so much reverence displayed by God’s servants as to check impure and virulent tongues, that nothing more monstrous can be imagined than what was here laid to Paul’s charge, and that we should bear the like evil without ceasing constantly to defend the genuine confession of the gospel.

Clarke keeps the dialogue running and gives the objection to the Jew: may we not suppose that our unrighteousness serves to commend and illustrate the mercy of God in keeping and fulfilling the promise made to our forefathers, so that the more wicked we are the more his faithfulness is to be admired, and if so, would not God appear unjust in taking vengeance and casting us off? The parenthesis he explains as feeling for the situation of himself and his countrymen, so that it is natural for one to speak so. The Apostle’s reply he renders as by no means: God cannot be unjust, and were he unjust he could not be qualified to judge the world nor to inflict that punishment on the unfaithful Jews to which the argument refers. The Jew resumes: if the faithfulness of God in keeping his promise is, through our unfaithfulness, made far more glorious than it otherwise would have been, why should we be blamed for what redounds so much to the honour of God? And the Apostle answers by pressing the consequence: why do you not say, seeing you assume this ground, that in all cases we should do wickedly, because God by freely pardoning can so glorify his own grace? This Clarke calls a most impious sentiment which nevertheless follows from the objector’s reasoning, and one injuriously laid to the charge of the apostles who preach the doctrine of free pardon through faith without the merit of works, so manifest a perversion of the truth that a just punishment may be expected to fall on the propagators of such a slander. Wesley states the objection plainly, that if our unrighteousness is subservient to God’s glory it seems unjust in him to punish us for it, and glosses the parenthesis as human weakness would be apt to speak. The answer he takes from the universality of the case, since all the unrighteousness in the world will then commend the righteousness of God. The restated objection he presses to its end, whether this can be said to be any sin at all, and whether one ought not to do what would otherwise be evil that so much good may come; to which, he says, the apostle does not deign to give a direct answer but cuts the objector short with a severe reproof.

Barnes sets out the objection in steps: it had been conceded that some had sinned, God’s character was unchanged notwithstanding, and in the very midst of sin his character as a just Being shone out illustriously; the question then is how he can punish the sin from which his own glory resulted, a question sinners often ask. To commend is to show forth or render illustrious, and the effect on David’s mind was that he saw the justice of God in his threatenings more clearly because of his own transgression. The clause about vengeance he renders as simply inflicting punishment, the idea of vengeance not being necessarily in the original word, which often means punishment without reference to the state of mind of him who inflicts it; and the parenthesis he takes as the language of an objector, implying a degree of reverence and a seeming unwillingness to state an objection dishonourable to God, so that no way of stating it could have been more artful or impressive. To judge, he explains, implies the possibility and correctness of condemning the guilty, since otherwise judgment would be a farce; and it is remarkable that the apostle neither attempts to explain how God could take occasion from the sins of men to promote his glory nor even admits the fact, but meets the objection directly, its force resting on the admitted point, taught in their own writings, that God would judge the world. He adds that God will judge offences from the nature of the crime itself and not from what he may do in overruling them: the punishment of a murderer is determined by the law and by his own desert, not by any reputation for integrity the judge may manifest at the trial, nor any honour accruing to the police for detecting him, nor any security resulting to the commonwealth from his execution, and none of these should be pleaded in bar of his condemnation. The truth of God he refers to his faithfulness in adhering to his threatenings, so that every lost sinner will be an eternal monument of it, and the lie to falsehood or unfaithfulness. The flaw in the objector’s reasoning he identifies exactly: he takes for granted that the direct tendency of his conduct is to promote God’s glory, whereas it is just the reverse, and it is by God’s reversing or overruling that tendency that he obtains his glory, as the tendency of murder is not to honour the law though the execution may. The answer to the last objection he takes to be the carrying of it out to its consequence, a result so shocking that stating it is refutation enough; the doctrines misrepresented were that the sins of men were the occasion of promoting God’s glory in the plan of salvation and that where sin abounded grace did much more abound. From this he draws a maxim never to be departed from, that a man is not to be held responsible for the inferences others draw from his doctrine and is answerable only for what he avows, and another, that evil is not to be done that good may come, whatever advantage to ourselves or to our cause or whatever glory to God we may think will result. Ellicott states the difficulty as a new and profound question which the Apostle’s keen intellect will not let go, that if the sin of man only tends to vindicate the righteousness of God there seems no reason why it should be punished; the mere raising of such a question requires an apology, and it is only as a man might speak about man that he dares to utter it. The objection he calls impossible, since if it held good there could be no judgment at all, no sin being punishable because all sin would emphasise the strict veracity of God in his denunciations of it and so conduce to his glory, and would thus cease to be sinful. He thinks Paul considers it a sufficient answer merely to propound the question about judging the world, since he and his readers all assumed a future judgment, and he compares the way Bishop Butler deals with the argument from necessity, substituting present for future judgment and observing that God does govern even brute creatures by rewards and punishments in the natural course of things, so that the necessitarian must either give up his opinion or harmonise it with these facts. Truth he takes in the first instance of God’s veracity as involved in his threats and promises and then of the attributes connected with it, especially justice, the word leaning towards its moral sense; and the lie, set as its antithesis, he calls the moral deflection that follows upon unbelief. In the last verse a phrase must be supplied, and the Apostle does not care to answer the argument in detail but will not dally with such a perversion of the moral sense; Ellicott asks what pretext anyone could have for attributing such an opinion to Paul, and answers that the charge was no doubt utterly false as applied to him but that his teaching was made an excuse for Antinomian excesses which would naturally be fastened upon him, or else that the Judaizing party argued that a man who openly breaks the Law and yet claims to be in the right way is doing evil that good may come. Robertson notes the rhetorical question as common with Paul when he surveys an argument, and that the verb rendered commendeth occurs in two senses, to introduce or commend and to prove or establish, either making good sense here; the participle he glosses as the inflicter of the anger, and the parenthesis as if to say, pardon me for this line of argument, remarking on Tholuck’s observation that the rabbis often used both these phrases and that Paul had not forgotten his rabbinical training. The next verse he says contains a suppressed condition between the two particles, since if that were true, how. The noun for lie occurs only here in the New Testament, the manuscripts differ over the opening particle, and Paul uses the first person from motives of delicacy, transferring the objection to himself by a fiction for argument’s sake. The last verse he calls a tangled sentence which can be cleared up in two ways, by supplying a deliberative subjunctive after the negative or by making a long parenthesis of everything between, a parenthesis being necessary in any case since there are two lines of thought, the excuse brought forward by the unbeliever and the accusation that Paul affirms that very excuse; and he finds it almost uncanny that the maxim later associated with the Jesuits should be attributed to Paul in the first century by Jews, the accusation being undoubtedly one of Antinomianism because he preached justification by faith and not by works.

Theodoret gives the objection in its own words and answers that it is one of the most absurd things thus to speak, for the sentence of God is just, and one’s own unworthiness cannot advance at all the glory arising to God for his kindness; it were the extremest injustice that they who advanced his glory should suffer vengeance from him and expect eternal punishment, which is what not even the most unjust of men would do, how far less he from whom flow the very fountains of righteousness.

debates: Whether the objection is answered or only recoiled from: Calvin holds that Paul gives no direct reply but expresses abhorrence, which he thinks weightier than a denial, and supplies the direct refutation himself; Barnes says Paul meets it head on, while noting it as remarkable that he neither explains nor concedes the fact; Ellicott and Wesley both say he does not deign to answer the last form of it at all.

What the verb rendered commend means: Robertson allows both to introduce or commend and to prove or establish, either making good sense; Gill restricts it to manifestation and illustration, and insists that unrighteousness illustrates the righteousness of God only by accident and never of its own nature.

Where the slander came from: Ellicott suspects either Antinomian excesses fastened on Paul’s teaching or a Judaizing complaint that a man who openly breaks the Law yet claims to be in the right way; Barnes traces it to a misrepresentation of the doctrine that where sin abounded grace did much more abound; Robertson simply calls it the accusation of Antinomianism.
outliers: Barnes answers the objection with a courtroom analogy, that a murderer is condemned by the law and his own desert and not acquitted because his trial displays the judge’s integrity or his execution secures the commonwealth.
Ellicott sets Bishop Butler’s reply to the argument from necessity alongside Paul’s question, substituting present for future judgment.

Robertson cites Tholuck’s observation that the rabbis used both of Paul’s formulae here, and finds it uncanny that the maxim later associated with the Jesuits should be laid at Paul’s door in the first century.

Calvin turns the calumny into a lesson for his own readers, that God’s servants have never displayed reverence enough to check virulent tongues, and that the like evil is to be borne without ceasing to defend the confession.
themes: how shall God judge the world
let us do evil that good may come

9.pericope_label: What then? are we better than they? No, in no wise: for we have before proved both Jews and Gentiles, that they are all under sin; as it is written, There is none righteous, no, not one: there is none that understandeth, there is none that seeketh after God. They are all gone out of the way, they are together become unprofitable; there is none that doeth good, no, not one

schools.summary: Gill takes the apostle to return to what he was treating at the beginning of the chapter, suggesting that though the Jew has the advantage of the Gentile with respect to some external privileges, he has none with regard to their state and condition God-ward and as in his sight. Of the quotations he observes that they are taken out of the Psalms and Isaiah and are brought to prove not only that the Jews are no better than the Gentiles, being equally corrupt, but also to show the corrupt state of mankind in general; the words are not always literally expressed but the sense is attended to, since the original says there is none that doeth good, from which the apostle rightly infers that there is none righteous, for he that does not do good is not righteous, and if there is none on earth that does good and does not sin, there is none righteous upon earth, no, not one single person. On the want of understanding he grants that man has not lost by sin the natural faculty of the understanding so as to become like the horse and mule which are without any, and allows that natural men have some understanding of things natural, civil and moral, though there is none who understands even these as Adam did; but they have no understanding of things spiritual, no spiritual knowledge of God, no true sense of their own sin and misery, no true knowledge of the way of salvation by Christ, and no experience of the work of the Spirit upon their souls. The going out of the way he expounds from the Hebrew, which he says means gone aside as persons in debt: man had a considerable stock of righteousness, holiness and knowledge, but has run through it all, contracted large and numerous debts, been obliged to hide himself and used as a bankrupt and turned out of house and home, though Christ undertook to pay and has paid all the debts of his people and put them into a better state than ever Adam was in; elsewhere it is rendered that every one is gone back, that is from God and from his commands, and here that they are all gone out of the way, out of the way of God and his precepts, out of the way of holiness and righteousness and of light and life, into their own ways, the ways of sin and Satan and the world of darkness and of death. Calvin explains that the apostle returns from his digression and now replies in what respect the Jews excelled the Gentiles; though the answer seems to militate against what he had said before, since he now strips those of all dignity to whom he had attributed so much, there is no discord, for the privileges in which he allowed them to be eminent were separate from themselves and dependent on God’s goodness and not on their own merit, whereas here he inquires as to their own worthiness and whether they could glory in any respect in themselves. Since it was their chief superiority that God’s oracles were deposited with them, and they had this not through their own merit, there was nothing left on account of which they could glory before God. He notes a holy contrivance in the pronouns, that when Paul ascribes pre-eminence to them he speaks in the third person, but when he strips them of all things he puts himself among them, that he might avoid giving offence. The verb of accusation he calls properly a forensic term and renders it we have brought a charge, since an accuser in an action is said to charge a crime which he is prepared to substantiate by testimonies and other proofs, and the apostle had summoned all mankind universally before the tribunal of God that he might include all under the same condemnation; to be under sin means that we are justly condemned as sinners before God, or held under the curse which is due to sin, for as righteousness brings with it absolution, so sin is followed by condemnation. Of the quotations he says that Paul, having hitherto used proofs or arguments to convince men of their iniquity, now begins to reason from authority, which is to Christians the strongest kind of proof when it is derived from the only true God; and hence let ecclesiastical teachers learn what their office is, for since Paul asserts no truth but what he confirms by the sure testimony of Scripture, much less ought such a thing to be attempted by those who have no other commission but to preach the gospel they have received. He observes that the Apostle gives the meaning rather than the entire words, stating generally the substance of what the Prophet declares before coming to particulars, and then enumerating the effects or fruits of this unrighteousness. The first effect he takes to be ignorance, since empty is the man in whom there is not the knowledge of God, whatever other learning he may possess, and the sciences and arts, which in themselves are good, are empty things when they are without this groundwork. By the word rendered unprofitable he understands that they had put off every feeling of humanity, for as the best bond of mutual concord among us is the knowledge of God, who as the common Father of all wonderfully unites us and without whom there is nothing but disunion, so inhumanity commonly follows where there is ignorance of God, every one when he despises others loving and seeking his own good.

Henry states the conclusion of the passage plainly, that all mankind are under the guilt of sin as a burden and under the government and dominion of sin as enslaved to it, to work wickedness, and that this is made plain by several passages of Scripture from the Old Testament which describe the corrupt and depraved state of all men till grace restrain or change them. Great as our advantages are, he adds, these texts describe multitudes who call themselves Christians, whose principles and conduct prove that there is no fear of God before their eyes; and where no fear of God is, no good is to be looked for.

Clarke gives the question to the Jew, whether after all the Jews have not a better claim to the privileges of the kingdom of God than the Gentiles have, and the answer to the Apostle, that he has already proved both Jews and Gentiles under the guilt of sin, equally unworthy of the blessings of the Messiah’s kingdom, and that both must equally owe their salvation to the mere mercy of God; and he observes that in order to enforce the conviction upon the heart of the Jew, Paul quotes his own Scriptures, which he acknowledged had been given by the inspiration of God and consequently true. The first citation he applies without restriction, holding it true not only of the Jews but of the Gentiles, of every soul of man considered in his natural and practical state previously to receiving the mercy of Christ, since there is no righteous principle in them and consequently no righteous act can be expected from them; God himself is represented as looking down from heaven to see if there were any that feared and sought after him, and yet he who cannot be deceived could find none, from which we may safely conclude there was none to be found. The turning aside he renders as diverging from the right way, the Jews in forsaking the law and the prophets and the Gentiles in acting contrary to the law God had written on their hearts, the departure of both proving the evil propensity of human nature in general; and the next word he glosses from the Hebrew as putrid, viewing the whole mass of mankind as slain and thrown together to putrefy in heaps, infected and infectious, which is what is termed the corruption of human nature. He distinguishes the two clauses, the earlier want of righteousness referring to the want of a righteous principle and the later want of good works to the necessary consequence of its absence, since if there be no righteousness within there will be no acts of goodness without. Wesley takes the whole to show that all men are under the guilt and power of sin, the Jews by transgressing the written law and the Gentiles by transgressing the law of nature, and defends the citations by noting that though David and Isaiah spoke primarily of their own age they expressed what manner of men God sees when he looks down from heaven, not what he makes them by his grace. He lays out the structure of the catena, the first line being the general proposition and the particulars following in order, the dispositions and designs, then the discourse, then the actions; the want of understanding he refers to the things of God, and the becoming unprofitable to being helpless and impotent, unable to profit either themselves or others.

Barnes treats the question as another remark supposed to be made by a Jewish objector, asking whether the Jews have any preference or advantage as to character and prospects over the Gentiles, and restricts it to the great point in debate, justification before God; he had admitted that the Jews had important advantages in some respects, but now affirms that those advantages made no difference about justification, since they had failed to keep the law and must be justified, if at all, in the same way as the rest of the world. Of the quotations he insists that the point to be proved is the depravity of the Jews and not universal depravity, that the interpretation should be confined to the bearing of the passages on the Jews, and that they should not be adduced as directly proving the doctrine of universal depravity, their direct reference being to the Jewish nation and their design being to show that this characteristic of sin was not confined to any period of their history but pertained to them as a people. Most of the passages, he notes, are quoted from the Greek version; the Hebrew of the first says there is none that doeth good, and the apostle quotes according to the sense with a word that accords with his argument; the closing phrase is not in the Hebrew but in the Greek, and is a strong universal expression denoting the state of almost universal corruption in the psalmist’s time, which should not be interpreted to mean that there was not literally one pious man in the nation but that the characteristic of the nation was that it was exceedingly corrupt. In the next verse he finds high poetic beauty and deep solemnity in the figure of God looking down from heaven to make investigation, and argues that though the Hebrew only implies that none such were found, the apostle states the fact, since none could escape God’s notice and the benevolence of his heart would have led him to record it had there been any. To understand he takes in the sense of being wise, or of having such a state of moral feeling as disposes men to serve and obey God, the word often denoting not a mere intellectual operation but the state of the heart; and a disposition not to seek after God he calls one of the most decided proofs of depravity, since a righteous man counts it his highest privilege to know God and a man can indulge in wickedness only by forgetting him. The next clause he explains as declining from the true path of piety and virtue, all being united in this declension, and the word for unprofitable as meaning in Hebrew to become putrid and offensive like fruit that is spoiled, or in Arabic milk that has soured, and applied to moral subjects to become corrupt and useless. Ellicott renders the question as whether we can claim a preference, notes that the form of the Greek verb is peculiar and takes it on the whole as middle for active, which would be apparently unexampled but is tenable as a question of language and seems compelled by the context; there is no real opposition, he adds, between the denial here and the much every way earlier, since there the reference was to external advantages and here to real and essential worth in the sight of God. For the verb of accusation he adopts the marginal rendering, that Paul before charged both Jews and Gentiles with being all under sin. The verses he calls a striking instance of the way the Apostle weaves together passages taken from different sources, and also an example of the corruptions in the text of the Old Testament to which the practice gave rise, since the whole passage as it stands here is found in some manuscripts of the Greek version as part of the fourteenth psalm, whence it has been copied not only into the Vulgate but into the Prayer Book, which differs from the Bible version. The quotations, he observes, have different degrees of appositeness so far as they may be considered probative rather than illustrative: the first is couched in such general terms as to be directly in point, the second and third are aimed specially against the oppressors of the Psalmist, the fourth likewise but in a more general form, that from Isaiah indicates the moral degradation among the prophet’s contemporaries that had led to the Captivity, and the last is an expression applied not to all men but particularly to the wicked. The word for unprofitable he takes to express a state of moral corruption, and together to mean altogether, the whole mass of mankind with one consent having fallen to ruin. Robertson notes the frequency of Paul’s opening query and calls the verb difficult and common, unsettled in sense: in the active it means to have before or to excel, but here it is middle or passive, Thayer taking it as middle to excel to one’s advantage and arguing that the context demands this though no example of the middle in that sense has been found, Lightfoot taking it as passive to mean are we excelled and finding that sense in Plutarch, and Vaughan taking it as passive but meaning are we preferred, which suits the context though no other example has been found; the papyri throw no light on it. The verb of accusation he parses as a first aorist middle of a word not yet found anywhere else, meaning to make a prior accusation, and refers it to the two preceding chapters. The quotation formula he notes as the usual one, and calls what follows a chain of citations to prove the point that Jews are in no better case than Greeks; Dr J. Rendel Harris has shown that the Jews and early Christians had collections of testimonies from the Old Testament strung together for certain purposes as proof-texts, and Paul may have used one of them or put these passages together himself. He gives the sources of each member of the chain, notes that Paul has given compounded quotations elsewhere, and remarks that this compounded quotation was imported bodily into the text of the Greek psalm in the chief manuscripts. The opening sentence he calls a motto for all the rest and a summary of what follows. The participle for understanding he parses as a late form, and the verb for becoming unprofitable as a late word found in Polybius and in a Cilician inscription of the first century, occurring only here in the New Testament, the Hebrew word meaning to go bad or become sour like milk.

Chrysostom explains why the argument turns back on itself: having accused the Gentiles and accused the Jews, it came next in order to mention the righteousness which is by faith, since if the law of nature availed not and the written Law was of no advantage, but both weighed down those who used them wrongly and made it plain that they were worthy of greater punishment, then the salvation which is by grace was necessary; but as yet Paul does not venture, having an eye to the violence of the Jews, and so turns afresh to his accusation of them. He brings in David speaking at length of the same things which Isaiah mentioned in short compass, furnishing a strong curb for them so that they might not bound off, nor any of his hearers start away when the matters of faith were laid open, being beforehand safely held down by the accusations of the prophets. Three excesses, he says, the prophet lays down: that all of them together did evil, that they did not do good indifferently along with evil but followed after wickedness alone, and that they followed it with all earnestness. Cyril reaches the same verse at the end of a survey of human wickedness: Cain and Abel succeeded in the second generation and Cain was the first murderer, a deluge was afterwards poured abroad because of the great wickedness of men, and fire came down from heaven upon the people of Sodom because of their transgression; after a time God chose out Israel, but Israel also turned aside and the chosen race was wounded, for while Moses stood before God in the mount the people were worshipping a calf instead of God, and in the lifetime of the law-giver who had said thou shalt not commit adultery a man dared to transgress. After Moses, prophets were sent to cure Israel, but in their healing office they lamented that they were not able to overcome the disease, so that one of them says that the godly man is perished out of the earth and there is none that doeth right among men, and again quotes the very words that all are gone out of the way and are together become unprofitable.

debates: How far the indictment reaches: Barnes confines it to the depravity of the Jews and warns that the passage should not be adduced as directly proving universal depravity; Clarke applies it without restriction to every soul of man in his natural state; Ellicott grades the citations, the first general enough to be directly in point and the last applied particularly to the wicked rather than to all men.

What the opening verb means: Robertson leaves it unsettled between a middle sense of excelling to one’s own advantage, Lightfoot’s passive are we excelled, and Vaughan’s are we preferred, noting that the papyri give no help; Ellicott takes it as middle for active, granting that this would be apparently unexampled but holding that the context compels it.

Whether the closing phrase is to be pressed: Barnes observes that it is absent from the Hebrew and drawn from the Greek, and denies that it means no pious man existed; Clarke argues that God who cannot be deceived looked and found none, so that we may safely conclude there were none.
outliers: Ellicott and Robertson both note that this compound quotation was afterwards imported bodily into the Greek text of the fourteenth psalm, Ellicott tracing it thence into the Vulgate and the Prayer Book as a specimen of the textual corruption such quoting produced.

Calvin observes a deliberate tact in the pronouns, Paul praising the nation in the third person and accusing it in the first, and turns the appeal to authority into a lesson for teachers, who have far less warrant than an apostle to assert anything unconfirmed by Scripture.
Gill allegorises the turning aside as the flight of a bankrupt who has run through his whole stock and been turned out of house and home, with Christ undertaking the debt.
Clarke reads the word for unprofitable as putrid and pictures the whole mass of mankind thrown together to putrefy in heaps, infected and infectious.

13.pericope_label: Their throat is an open sepulchre; with their tongues they have used deceit; the poison of asps is under their lips: whose mouth is full of cursing and bitterness: their feet are swift to shed blood: destruction and misery are in their ways: and the way of peace have they not known: there is no fear of God before their eyes

schools.summary: Gill takes the throat to be called an open sepulchre for its voracity and insatiableness, both as an instrument of speech, since the words of the wicked are devouring ones, and as an instrument of swallowing, denoting the sinner’s eager desire after sin, the delight he takes in it and his insatiable greediness for it; likewise for its filthy stench, the communication of evil men being corrupt, and because, as by an open grave persons may fall unawares to their hurt, so the evil communications of wicked men are dangerous and hurtful. He notes that Aben Ezra explains the phrase by immediate destruction or sudden death. The cursing he takes for the cursing of God, sometimes internal with the heart and sometimes external with the mouth, and of all good men, though without cause and to no purpose with respect to those they curse, since God has blessed them, and greatly to the cursers’ own detriment, since in the issue their curses will be turned against themselves; there is also a cursing of superiors, as parents, masters, magistrates and governors, which is a sore evil, and of themselves and their fellow creatures. That the mouth is full of it denotes the frequency of the sin, since scarce anything else comes out of it, which discovers the corruption of the heart, for out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaketh; and by bitterness he understands either sin in general, an evil and bitter thing in its nature and effects, or sinful words such as oaths, curses and imprecations. The swiftness of the feet he takes for the readiness and eagerness of men to murder innocent creatures, showing the malice that is in them, and thinks the words seem to point at the times of Manasseh, who shed so much innocent blood as to fill Jerusalem with it from one end to the other. Destruction and misery he understands either actively, that all the ways and methods they pursue are to make their fellow creatures miserable and to ruin them, or passively, that by their sinful course of life they are themselves brought to destruction and misery, since the way they walk in is the broad way that leads to destruction and its end is eternal death. Ignorance of the way of peace he extends widely: men are naturally ignorant of the way of peace with God, of the first step God took towards it, of the council and covenant of peace in which the scheme was drawn, of Christ the peacemaker and the way in which he made it, and of the Gospel which reveals it; they are ignorant of the way to enjoy peace of conscience, having no true peace of mind but often tortured consciences, or else a stupid and secure peace with nothing solid in it, being without the Spirit whose fruit is peace and without faith in Christ; and they are ready to think that peace must be had by doing something of their own. By the fear of God he says is meant not a fear of wrath and damnation, nor a fearful distrust of God’s presence, power, providence and grace, much less a hypocritical fear, but a reverential affection for God peculiar to the children of God, springing from a sense of divine goodness, attended with holiness of heart and life, consistent with faith and even with full assurance of it and with spiritual joy in its highest degree, standing opposed to pride and haughtiness and a blessing of the covenant of grace; and this is not to be found in unregenerate men, since it springs from grace and not nature and is implanted only in conversion, as appears from the whole life and conversation of unconverted men. Calvin takes the first figure to mean a gulf to swallow up men, which he says is more than calling them man-eaters, since it is an intimation of extreme barbarity that the throat should be so great a gulf as to swallow down and devour men whole and entire; he records that Stuart gives the figure differently, that as from the sepulchre issues an offensive and pestilential vapour so from the mouths of slanderous persons issue noisome and pestilential words. On the next citation he observes that Paul corrects the order of the words as found in the Greek and gives the Hebrew more exactly, while retaining the word bitterness by which the Greek had rendered a term meaning mischievous deceit, and that some would emend the Hebrew accordingly though no copy favours it; the vice is of an opposite character to the former, the meaning being that they are in every way full of wickedness, for if they speak fair they deceive and blend poison with their flatteries, but if they draw forth what they have in their hearts, bitterness and cursing stream out. The verses from Isaiah he calls very striking, noting that Paul has abbreviated both the Hebrew and the Greek, changed two words of the Greek version and followed it in leaving out innocent before blood; the representation is of a ferociousness above measure barbarous, which produces solitude and waste by destroying everything wherever it prevails. Of the ignorance of peace he says that they are so habituated to plunders, acts of violence and wrong, to savageness and cruelty, that they know not how to act kindly and courteously. In the last clause he repeats what he had noticed at the beginning, that every wickedness flows from a disregard of God, for as the principal part of wisdom is the fear of God, when we depart from that there remains in us nothing right or pure; it is a bridle to restrain our wickedness, and when it is wanting we feel at liberty to indulge every kind of licentiousness. He then defends each testimony from its own context, arguing that the character of men is here described in order that we may see what man is when left to himself, since Scripture testifies that all men are in this state who are not regenerated by the grace of God; the condition of the saints would be nothing better were not this depravity corrected in them, and that they may remember they differ nothing from others by nature they find in the relics of their flesh the seeds of those evils, which would constantly produce fruit were they not mortified, for which mortification they are indebted to God’s mercy and not to their own nature; and though all the vices enumerated are not conspicuous in every individual, they may justly and truly be ascribed to human nature.

Clarke raises the textual question, observing that this and all the following verses to the end of the section are found in the Septuagint but not in the Hebrew text, and that it is most evident the apostle quoted from that version, since the verses cannot be found elsewhere with so near an approximation to his meaning and words; they are not, however, in the Alexandrian manuscript, though they exist in the Vulgate, the Ethiopic and the Arabic, and since the most ancient copies of the Septuagint do not contain them, some contend that the apostle quoted from different parts of Scripture and that later transcribers, finding the earlier verses taken from the fourteenth psalm, imagined the rest were found there too and incorporated them into their copies from the apostle’s text. The first figure he refers to defamation, that by their malicious and wicked words they bury as it were the reputation of all men, the whole verse belonging to their habit of lying, slandering and blasting the reputation of others. Of the cursing he says they never speak but in profane oaths, blasphemies and malice; of the swift feet, that they make use of every means in their power to destroy the reputation and lives of the innocent; and of the next clause, that destruction is their work and misery to themselves and to the objects of their malice the consequence of their impious and murderous conduct. Ignorance of peace he takes both ways, that they neither have peace in themselves nor suffer others to live in quiet, being brooders and fomenters of discord. The last line he says completes their bad character, since they are downright atheists, at least practically such, fearing not God’s judgments although his eye is upon them; and he adds that there is not one article of the charge which may not be justified from the histories of Jews and Gentiles alike, and that what was true of them then is true still, appealing to the state of Europe between 1792 and 1814, the destruction of millions and the misery of hundreds of millions, the widows and orphans left to deplore their dead, and tracing it all to the evil desires of men, the lust of dominion, the insatiable thirst for money and the desire to be sole and independent, the same sin that ruined our first parents and proves us their legitimate offspring. Wesley observes the progress of evil discourse, proceeding out of the heart, through the throat, tongue and lips, till the whole mouth is filled with it, and notes that the poison is under the lips where honey is on them, backbiting and tale-bearing being infectious and deadly. The cursing he refers to God and the bitterness to the neighbour; the way of peace he says can only spring from righteousness; and to the last line he adds that much less is the love of God in their heart.

Barnes traces the first citation to the fifth psalm, quoted literally from the Greek, and notes that the psalm reproves those who were false, traitorous and slanderous, so that the expressions are to be interpreted accordingly. The sentiment may be that as the grave is ever open to receive all into destruction, so the throat of the slanderer is ever open to swallow up the peace and happiness of all, or that as from an open sepulchre there proceeds an offensive and pestilential vapour, so from the mouths of slanderous persons there proceed noisome and ruinous words; he judges the connection to demand the former. The asp he describes as a species of serpent whose poison is of such active operation that it kills almost the instant it penetrates, and without remedy, small and commonly concealed, often in the sand of a road, striking the traveller before he sees it, found chiefly in Egypt and Libya, and he recalls that Cleopatra is said to have suffered an asp to bite her rather than be carried captive to Rome; the poison is contained in a small bag concealed at the root of the tooth and pressed out through a small hole when the tooth strikes the flesh, though whether the psalmist knew this cannot be known. The next citation he says is not quoted literally but according to the sense, the psalm having deceits where Paul has bitterness, a word used to denote severity, harshness and cruelty. The three following verses he calls an abridgment of a passage in Isaiah, the apostle selecting a few expressions and making a reference to the entire passage rather than a formal quotation; the swift feet denote the eagerness of the nation to commit crime, thirsting for the blood of innocence and hasting to shed it. Destruction and misery he refers to the ruin they cause in the reputation, happiness and peace of others, the tendency of their conduct being to destroy the virtue and peace of all with whom they come in contact; and the ignorance of peace to their disregard of whatever would promote their own happiness or that of others, being intent on plans of evil. Fear in the last line he takes to denote reverence, awe and veneration, and observes that their conduct shows they are not withheld from iniquity by any regard to the fear or favour of God. He then draws five conclusions: that the quotations fully establish the position that the nation was far from righteous, being drawn from no less than six distinct places referring to different periods of their history, so that a Jew could not hope to be saved simply because he was a Jew; that they show how to use the Old Testament and the facts of ancient history, adduced not to show directly what the character of man is now but what human nature is, and as proofs of its tendency; that the view of depravity given is striking, confined to no one faculty or set of actions, since tongue, mouth, feet and lips are all involved and the entire man is corrupt; that if such was the character of the Jewish nation under all its advantages we are prepared to credit what is said of the state of the heathen world; and that the resulting view of human nature is melancholy from whatever quarter it is contemplated, a ruin over which we should sit down and weep while lifting our eyes in gratitude to the God of mercy who has devised a plan by which these ruins may be built again. Ellicott renders the first figure as speech at once corrupt and corrupting, compared to a yawning grave, not merely a pit into which a man may fall but a sort of pestiferous chasm yawning and ravening after its prey; the deceiving he renders strictly as a continued action brought up to the present, and the lips he explains from the poison-bag of the serpent lying directly under the tooth by which its venom is discharged. Bitterness he glosses as malignity, from the notion that venom was contained in the gall. Of the last line he observes that the fear of God, which is properly a subjective feeling, is here projected and regarded as an external rule of life. Robertson identifies the first noun as the old word for larynx and the second phrase as an opened grave, so that their words are like the odour of a newly opened grave, quoting the remark that some portions of Greek and Roman literature stink like a newly opened grave. The verb for using deceit he parses as an imperfect and not a perfect or aorist as the English implies, a word found only in the Greek Old Testament and here, with an ending once thought purely Alexandrian because so common in that version but in fact common in the Boeotian and Aeolic dialects, the Hebrew reading that they smoothed their tongues. Poison he notes is the old word for both rust and venom, and the word for asps is the common one for a round shield and then for the Egyptian cobra. The word for destruction he calls rare, from a verb meaning to rub together or crush, used elsewhere of a fracture and so in the papyri, and the word for misery common though occurring only here; wherever they go, he adds, they leave a trail of woe and destruction. The preposition of the last line he identifies as a late double compound found in the Greek Old Testament, in Polybius, and in papyri and inscriptions.

debates: What the open sepulchre figures: Barnes reports both the swallowing sense, the grave open to receive all into destruction, and the sense of a pestilential vapour issuing from the mouth, and judges the connection to require the first, as does Calvin, who makes the throat a gulf wide enough to devour men whole; Robertson takes the second, that their words carry the odour of a newly opened grave.

Whether these verses stand in the Hebrew: Clarke observes that they are found in the Greek version but not in the Hebrew text and are absent from the Alexandrian manuscript, and reports the theory that later transcribers imported them into their psalters from the apostle’s own text; Calvin instead traces each member to its original and marks where Paul follows the Greek, where he corrects its order by the Hebrew, and where he abbreviates.

Whom the indictment covers: Barnes holds that the citations prove the nation was not righteous and are to be used as evidence for the tendency of human nature rather than as a direct account of any man now; Clarke applies the whole without restriction to Jew and Gentile alike and to his own century; Calvin argues that the character described is what man is when left to himself, the saints differing only by a mortification they owe to grace.
