outliers: Barnes describes the asp at length, its concealment in the sand, its range in Egypt and Libya, the poison-bag at the root of the tooth, and the story that Cleopatra chose its bite over captivity in Rome.
Robertson quotes the remark that some portions of Greek and Roman literature stink like a newly opened grave.
Clarke leaves the text for the wars of Europe between 1792 and 1814, the millions destroyed and the widows and orphans left, tracing it all to the lust of dominion and the thirst for money.
Wesley notes that the poison lies under the lips where honey lies on them, and traces the progress of evil discourse from the heart through throat and tongue until the whole mouth is filled.

19.pericope_label: Now we know that what things soever the law saith, it saith to them who are under the law: that every mouth may be stopped, and all the world may become guilty before God. Therefore by the deeds of the law there shall no flesh be justified in his sight: for by the law is the knowledge of sin

schools.summary: Gill defines the law here as neither the law of nature, nor the civil law of nations, nor the ceremonial law of the Jews, nor barely the five books of Moses, nor the book of Psalms or the Prophets or the writings of the whole Old Testament, but the moral law as it appears in the whole word of God, which every man is bound to observe, of which all are transgressors, by which is the knowledge of sin, which no man can be justified by, and which Christ was made under and came to fulfil; and he notes that the law is represented as a person speaking, the phrase the law says being usual with Jewish writers. From the stopping of mouths he infers that there can be no justification before God by the law, since it stops the mouths of men and pronounces them guilty. By the deeds of the law he understands works done in obedience to it as performed by sinful men, which are very imperfect, not as performed by Adam in innocence or by Christ in our nature, whose works were perfect, but as performed by sinful men of themselves, and not as performed in and by Christ for them, who is the fulfilling end of the law for righteousness to all believers; and by such works, whether wrought before or after conversion, with or without the strength and grace of Christ, no man is justified. Calvin observes that Paul, leaving the Gentiles, addresses his words distinctly to the Jews, having a much more difficult work in subduing them, because they, though no less destitute of true righteousness than the Gentiles, covered themselves with the cloak of God’s covenant, as though it were a sufficient holiness to have been separated from the rest of the world by the election of God; and he anticipates their evasions, since whatever was said in the law unfavourably of mankind they usually applied to the Gentiles, as though they were exempt from the common condition of men. He shows from Scripture that they were not only blended with the multitude but that condemnation was peculiarly denounced on them, since to whom but the Jews had the law been given, and to whose instruction ought it to have served; what it states respecting others is as it were accidental, an appendage, but it applies its teaching mainly to its own disciples, and under the word law he includes also the Prophets and so the whole of the Old Testament. The stopping of the mouth he calls a metaphor taken from courts of law, where the accused, if he has anything to plead as a lawful defence, demands leave to speak that he might clear himself, but if he is convicted by his own conscience he is silent and without a word waits for his condemnation, being already by his own silence condemned, as when Job says that he will lay his hand on his mouth; and according to another sense, to be silent before the Lord is to tremble at his majesty and to stand mute, astonished at his brightness. The two closing clauses he takes to have been added not so much to include the Gentiles as to include the Jews who thought themselves exempted, no doubt the Gentiles being included but the special object being to prevent the Jews from supposing they were not. On the works of the law he records that it is a matter of doubt even among the learned, some extending them to the observance of the whole law and others confining them to the ceremonies alone, the addition of the word law having induced Chrysostom, Origen and Jerome to assent to the latter opinion, since they thought there is a peculiar intimation in that appendage that the expression should not be understood as including all works. The difficulty he thinks easily removed, for seeing that works are so far just before God as we seek by them to render to him worship and obedience, in order expressly to take away the power of justifying from all works he has mentioned those, if there be any, which can possibly justify, since the law has promises without which there would be no value in our works before God; it is by the law that a reward is apportioned to works, as the schoolmen knew when they held that works have no intrinsic worthiness but become meritorious by covenant, and though they were mistaken in not seeing that works are ever polluted with vices which deprive them of merit, the principle remains true that the reward for works depends on the free promise of the law. He answers the arguments drawn from circumcision and from the Epistle to the Galatians, and concludes that Paul speaks here of the whole law, this being a truth deserving to be remembered as the first in importance, that by keeping the law no one can attain righteousness, since all being guilty of transgression are condemned for unrighteousness by the law, and to be justified by works and to be guilty of transgressions are wholly inconsistent. From the last clause he reasons from what is of an opposite character, that righteousness is not brought to us by the law because it convinces us of sin and condemns us, for life and death proceed not from the same fountain; the argument holds only if we hold as an unvarying circumstance that by showing man his sin the law cuts off the hope of salvation. The law is indeed by itself, as it teaches us what righteousness is, the way to salvation, but our depravity and corruption prevent it from being of any advantage to us in this respect; and whosoever is found to be a sinner is deprived of righteousness, so that to devise with the sophisters a half kind of righteousness, so that works in part justify, is frivolous.

Henry infers from the whole that it is in vain to look for justification by the works of the law and that it is to be had only by faith, and he argues first from man’s guiltiness: we can never be justified and saved by the law that we have broken, as a convicted traitor can never come off by pleading the statute he has broken, for that law discovers his crime and condemns him, and if he had never broken it he might have been justified by it, but now there is no way of coming off but by pleading the act of indemnity and casting himself upon it. The guilt he fastens particularly on the Jews, who made their boast of the law and set up for justification by it, since this conviction belongs to them as well as others, being written in their own law; and he extends it in general to all the world, all of whom must plead guilty, those who stand most upon their own justification being certainly cast. He observes the method God takes both in justifying and in condemning, that he stops every mouth, those who are justified having their mouths stopped by a humble conviction and those who are condemned having their mouths stopped too, since they shall at last be convinced and sent speechless to hell; and he calls guilty before God a dreadful word, before an all-seeing God who cannot be deceived in his judgment and a righteous judge who will by no means clear the guilty. To drive us further from expecting justification by the law he ascribes this conviction to the law itself, since that law which convicts and condemns us can never justify us: the law is the straight rule which points out the right and the wrong, and it is the proper use and intendment of the law to open our wound and therefore not likely to be the remedy, since that which is searching is not sanative; those who would know sin must get the knowledge of the law in its strictness, extent and spiritual nature, and if we compare our own hearts and lives with the rule we shall discover wherein we have turned aside. On the last verse he observes two things: that no flesh shall be justified, no corrupted man, since the corruption that remains in our nature will for ever obstruct any justification by our own works, which, coming from flesh, must needs taste of the cask; and that it is in his sight, since he does not deny the justification which was by the deeds of the law in the sight of the church, they being in their church-estate a holy people and a nation of priests, but as the conscience stands in relation to God we cannot be justified by the deeds of the law.

Clarke argues that the word law here does not mean the Pentateuch, as is evident from the preceding quotations, not one of which is taken from that work; either the term must mean the Jewish writings in general, or that rule of moral conduct which God had given to both Jews and Gentiles, to the former in their own Scriptures and to the latter in the law written in their hearts by his own Spirit and acknowledged in their written codes and in their pleadings in every civil case. According to this great law, whether given in a written revelation as to the Jews or by the secret inspiration of his Spirit as in certain cases to the Gentiles, every mouth must be stopped and the whole world, both Jews and Gentiles, stand convicted before God, for all mankind have sinned against it. On the score of obedience to this moral law, he says, no human being shall be justified, none can be accepted in the sight of God; and the reason is that by the law is the knowledge of sin, it being that which ascertains what sin is, shows how men have deviated from its righteous demands, and sentences them to death because they have broken it. The law is thus properly considered as the rule of right, and unless God had given some such means of discovering what sin is, the darkened heart of man could never have formed an adequate conception of it; for as an acknowledged straight edge is the only way in which the straightness or crookedness of a line can be determined, so the moral obliquity of human actions can only be determined by the law of God, that rule of right which proceeds from his own immaculate holiness. Wesley takes the law here for the Old Testament, and observes that it speaks to those who own its authority, that is to the Jews and not the Gentiles, since Paul quoted no scripture against the Gentiles but pleaded with them only from the light of nature. Every mouth he glosses as full of bitterness and yet of boasting, and becoming guilty as being fully convicted and apparently liable to most just condemnation, adding that these things were written of old and quoted by Paul not to make men criminal but to prove them so. By the works of the law he understands the ground that a man has kept the law, chiefly the moral part of it, which alone is not abolished; and it is not without reason, he says, that Paul so often mentions the works of the law, whether ceremonial or moral, for it was on these only that the Jews relied, being wholly ignorant of those that spring from faith. By the law, he concludes, is only the knowledge of sin, but no deliverance either from the guilt or the power of it.

Barnes takes the stopping of mouths to denote that the argument for the depravity of the Jews from the Old Testament was so clear and satisfactory that nothing could be alleged in reply, and regards the verse as the conclusion of the whole argument, the expressions referring not to the Jews only but to all the world: the Gentiles are proved guilty by their own deeds and by a violation of the laws of nature, the Jews have been shown guilty by appeals to their own law and by arguments drawn from authority they admit, and thus the mouths of both are stopped. He therefore refers the purpose clause not particularly to the argument from the Jewish law but to the whole previous train of reasoning, so that the conclusion is general, drawn from arguments adapted to the two great divisions of mankind; all the world means all by nature, all who are out of Christ, all who are not pardoned. They are not made guilty by the law, he adds, but the argument from the law and from fact proves that they are. The word rendered guilty he takes from courts of justice, applied to a man who has not vindicated or defended himself, against whom the indictment is found true and who is in consequence subject to punishment, the idea being subjection to punishment always because the man personally deserves it, and never a mere obligation to punishment; the word is not elsewhere used in the New Testament nor found in the Greek Old Testament. From the whole he draws two conditions of guilt, that there must be a law, either of nature or by revelation, and that there must be a violation of that law chargeable on men as individuals for which they are personally responsible. By the deeds of the law he understands works such as the law requires, and shows from the course of the argument that the reference is to the rules by which Jews and Gentiles pretended to frame their lives, and in both cases not to ceremonial or ritual laws but to the moral law, whether made known by reason or by revelation, since the question discussed was not whether they had obeyed their ceremonial law but whether they had been found holy. Nor did he intend to speak of external works only, since he charges them throughout with a want of conformity of the heart no less than of the life; the conclusion is therefore general, that by no law made known by reason, conscience, tradition or revelation could man be justified. No flesh he calls a strong expression denoting the absolute universality of the conclusion, and in his sight refers to God sitting as a judge to determine the characters of men. Law he defines as a rule of action whose effect when applied to our conduct is to show us what sin is, so that a man may esteem himself very right until he compares himself with a rule; the more closely and faithfully it is applied the more he will see it, and so far from being justified by it he will be the more condemned, which is the way in which a sinner is converted. Ellicott explains that in order to bring the testimony of Scripture home to the Jews, and to prevent any subterfuge by which they might shift the reference on to the Gentiles, the Apostle calls attention to the fact that the Law, that is the Old Testament from which he has been quoting, speaks especially to those to whom it was given; he notes that different Greek words are used for the two verbs of speaking, the first applicable as much to the matter as to the utterance and the second referring specially to the outward act by which it is enunciated to certain persons. The last phrase he renders guilty to God, the dative expressing the person to whom the penalty is due. The opening word of the next verse he renders because rather than therefore, since all mankind alike owe the penalty for their sins because not even the Law can protect its votaries, having no power to justify but only to expose in its true colours the sinfulness of sin; the proposition is thrown into a general form, not by the works of the Jewish Law but by works of law, that is by any works done in obedience to any law, since law in the abstract is unable to justify, and though it might perhaps if men could really keep it, no law can be kept strictly and entirely. The knowledge of sin he glosses as full and thorough knowledge, since in the state anterior to law man is not supposed to know what is sinful and what is not, conscience gradually developed giving him some insight into the distinction while the full knowledge of right and wrong in all its details is reserved for the introduction of positive law; law has however only this enlightening faculty, holding the mirror up to guilt without being able to remove it. Robertson parses the purpose clause with an old verb meaning to fence in or block up, remarks that stopping mouths is a difficult business, and observes that Paul seems here to be speaking directly to Jews, the hardest to convince, so that with the previous proof he covers the whole ground, having made the case against the Gentiles earlier. The phrase for becoming guilty he renders as becoming answerable to God, an old forensic word occurring only here in the New Testament, so that every one is liable in God’s court. The next phrase he renders out of works of law, meaning the Mosaic law and any law as the source of being set right with God, and notes that Paul quotes the psalm as he had done in another epistle to prove his point; the effect of law universally, he adds, is rebellion to it, and he has now proven the guilt of both Gentile and Jew.

Theodoret finds the wording of the first clause chosen with the greatest accuracy of expression, in that Paul puts it not concerning those who are under the law but to those who are under the law; for it speaks much concerning the Babylonians and Persians and Medes and Egyptians and many other nations, but nevertheless even these predictions concerning them it addresses to the Jews. The purpose clause he says employs the word that according to Paul’s favourite idiom, for the God of all did not bestow laws and send forth his exhortations among men in order that he might render them obnoxious to punishment, but consulting for their salvation has he done this; it is they themselves who by pursuing an opposite course have drawn this vengeance on themselves. Of the works of the law he distinguishes two kinds: some of the injunctions of the Mosaic law agreed with the knowledge of nature, such as the commands not to commit adultery, to do no murder, not to steal, not to bear false witness and to honour father and mother, for they who had never received that law were yet fully aware that each of these deserved not only condemnation but punishment likewise; and some the Lawgiver imposed on the Jews as suitable to them for that present time only, such as circumcision and the sabbath and sacrifices and sprinklings and the rites respecting the leper and the unclean, which are symbols of other things and, when fulfilled, are not in themselves sufficient to make the doer just. Wherefore the apostle says that by the works of the law there shall no flesh be justified in his sight, and then, lest anyone should suppose he was passing a censure on the law, adds that by the law is the knowledge of sin.

debates: What the works of the law are: Calvin reports the learned divided, names Chrysostom, Origen and Jerome for confining the phrase to ceremonies, and argues for the whole law, since Paul names precisely those works which could conceivably justify; Barnes and Wesley take the moral law to be meant; Ellicott generalises to works done in obedience to any law whatever; Theodoret divides the Mosaic injunctions into those that agree with what nature already knows and those imposed for that time only.

Whom the closing clauses are aimed at: Calvin holds they were added not so much to bring in the Gentiles as to include the Jews who thought themselves exempt; Barnes refers the purpose clause back over the whole preceding argument, so that the conclusion is universal and drawn from proofs adapted to both divisions of mankind; Wesley restricts what the law says to those who own its authority, since Paul had pleaded with the Gentiles only from the light of nature.

Whether the law is of any use toward righteousness: Henry says that what is searching is not sanative, the law opening the wound and therefore unlikely to be the remedy; Calvin grants that the law is in itself the way to salvation as it teaches what righteousness is, only our corruption preventing it; Ellicott says it holds the mirror up to guilt but cannot remove it.
outliers: Henry compares the man who looks for justification by a broken law to a convicted traitor pleading the very statute that condemns him, whose only recourse is the act of indemnity.

Calvin allows a second sense for the stopped mouth besides the forensic one, that to be silent before the Lord is to tremble at his majesty and stand mute at his brightness, and he notes the schoolmen’s maxim that works have no intrinsic worthiness but become meritorious by covenant.
Clarke compares the law to a straight edge, the only means by which a line can be shown crooked, and holds that without it the darkened heart could never have conceived what sin is.
Barnes notes that the word rendered guilty occurs nowhere else in the New Testament and not at all in the Greek Old Testament, and always implies that the punishment is personally deserved.

21.pericope_label: But now the righteousness of God without the law is manifested, being witnessed by the law and the prophets; even the righteousness of God which is by faith of Jesus Christ unto all and upon all them that believe: for there is no difference: for all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God

schools.summary: Gill takes the apostle, having proved that all men are unrighteous and that none can be justified by obedience to the law of nature or of Moses, to proceed to the righteousness which does justify, the revelation of which is peculiar to the Gospel. Of the faith by which it comes he says it is not that faith which Christ himself had as man but that of which he is the author and object, noting that the Alexandrian copy reads faith in Jesus Christ; and he denies faith any causal role, since it is neither the efficient nor the moving nor the meritorious cause of justification, nor even the instrumental cause of it on the part of God or Christ, nor is it the matter of a justifying righteousness, being a part of sanctification, itself imperfect, a man’s own as implanted in him and exercised by him, and elsewhere distinguished from righteousness, which is the obedience and blood of Christ; faith is rather a means of apprehending and receiving righteousness, viewing the excellency of Christ’s righteousness and owning it. Of the last clause he says that all have sinned in Adam, are guilty by his sin, polluted with it and condemned for it, and are sinners in themselves by their own actual transgressions, this being the case of the whole world and of all men in it, not only of the Gentiles but of the Jews and the more righteous among them; hence there is no difference in the state and condition of men by nature, nor any reason in themselves why God saves one and not another, nor any room to despair of the grace and righteousness of Christ on account of being in one’s own view the worst of sinners. Calvin says it is not certain for what distinct reason Paul calls that the righteousness of God which we obtain by faith, whether because it alone can stand before God or because the Lord in his mercy confers it on us, and since both interpretations are suitable he contends for neither. The law from which it is free he understands as meaning works, since it is not proper to refer the word to the law’s teaching, which is immediately adduced as bearing witness to the gratuitous righteousness of faith; some confine it to ceremonies, a view he calls unsound and frigid. The merits of works are therefore excluded, and Paul does not blend works with the mercy of God but, having wholly removed all confidence in works, sets up mercy alone. He records that Augustine explained it differently, taking the righteousness of God for the grace of regeneration and excluding only those works by which men of themselves endeavour without renovation to oblige God; but that the Apostle includes all works without exception, even those which the Lord produces in his own people, Calvin thinks evident from the context, since Abraham was regenerated and led by the Spirit at the very time when he denied that he was justified by works. The remission of sins alone is therefore set down as the cause of righteousness, and the consciences of men will never be tranquillised until they rest on the mercy of God alone; nor can this be confined to the commencement of justification, since the same definition applied to David after long service and to Abraham thirty years after his call, and since the conscience performs its office not for one day only but through life, so that we cannot remain even to death in a justified state except we look to Christ only. The opening particle he allows to be taken either adversatively or as an adverb of time, and taking the latter he denies that the abrogation of ceremonies alone is meant, since the design was to illustrate by comparison the grace in which we excel the fathers; it does not follow that the righteousness was hidden before Christ came, for a twofold manifestation is to be noticed, the first in the Old Testament by the word and the sacraments and the other in the New, which contains the completion of ceremonies and promises as exhibited in Christ himself, the gospel giving it a fuller brightness. The witness of the law he says is added lest the gospel should seem to militate against the law: as Paul has denied that the righteousness of faith needs the law’s aid, so he now asserts that it is confirmed by its testimony, and if the law affords testimony to gratuitous righteousness it is evident the law was not given to teach men how to obtain righteousness by works, so that they pervert it who turn it to such a purpose; examine the chief things taught by Moses, he says, and you will find that man cast from the kingdom of God had no other restoration from the beginning than that contained in the evangelical promises through the blessed seed, a demonstration of iniquity in the commandments, and in the sacrifices the lesson that satisfaction and cleansing are to be obtained in Christ alone. The genitive of faith he explains as meaning not the faith which is Christ’s but the faith of which he is the object, an Hebraism of frequent occurrence which ought to be rendered faith in Jesus Christ; and by introducing again the name of God, Paul seems to make God the founder and not only the approver of this righteousness, so that it flows from him alone and is made manifest to us in Christ. The question of justification is therefore to be referred not to the judgment of men but to the judgment of God, before whom nothing is counted righteousness but perfect and absolute obedience to the law; and since no one has attained such a measure, all are in themselves destitute of righteousness and Christ must come to our aid, who being alone just can render us just by transferring to us his own righteousness. When we are justified, the efficient cause is the mercy of God, the meritorious is Christ, and the instrumental is the word in connection with faith; faith is said to justify because it is the instrument by which we receive Christ, in whom righteousness is conveyed to us, and having been made partakers of Christ we ourselves are not only just but our works also are counted just, their imperfections being obliterated by his blood. The doubled phrase he takes as a repetition for the sake of amplifying, that Paul might more fully express that faith alone is required, that the faithful are not distinguished by external marks, and that it matters not whether they be Gentiles or Jews; he reports the view that the righteousness came to the Jews as promised to them and to the Gentiles as a gift with which they were unacquainted, but holds that the possession was equal and belonged to all who believed and to none else.

Henry asks whether guilty man must remain under wrath and whether the wound is for ever incurable, and answers that another way is laid open: this is the righteousness of God, of his ordaining and providing and accepting, obtained by that faith which has Jesus Christ for its object, an anointed Saviour, justifying faith respecting Christ in all his three anointed offices as Prophet, Priest and King, trusting in him, accepting him and cleaving to him. In all these, he says, Jews and Gentiles are alike welcome to God through Christ; there is no difference, and his righteousness is not only offered to those who believe but put upon them as a crown and as a robe. It is free grace and mere mercy, with nothing in us to deserve such favours; it comes freely to us, but Christ bought it and paid the price. Of the failure he says that all are sinners by nature and by practice and have come short of the glory of God, having failed of that which is the chief end of man; they come short as the archer comes short of the mark and as the runner comes short of the prize, so as not only not to win but to be great losers. He divides the failure three ways: they come short of glorifying God, since man was placed at the head of the visible creation actively to glorify his Creator and by sin dishonours him instead; they come short of glorying before God, since there is no boasting of innocency and the fact that we have all sinned is an everlasting estoppel, for we may glory before short-sighted men but not before him who cannot endure to look upon iniquity; and they come short of being glorified by God, of justification which is glory begun and of the holiness which is his glorious image upon man, having overthrown all hope of being glorified with God in heaven by any righteousness of their own, since it is impossible now to get to heaven in the way of spotless innocency, that passage being blocked up and a cherub with a flaming sword set to keep the way to the tree of life.

Clarke says God’s method of saving sinners is now shown by the Gospel to be through his own mere mercy by Christ Jesus, without the law, that is without any right or claim which might result from obedience to it, and that this is evidently what was intended by God from the beginning, since it is witnessed by the law and the prophets, the rites and ceremonies of the one and the preachings and predictions of the others all bearing testimony to the great design of God and to the absolute necessity of the salvation he has provided. The righteousness is not restrained to any particular people, as the law and its privileges were, but is unto all mankind in its intention and offer and becomes effectual to them that believe, God having now made no difference between Jews and Gentiles. On the last clause he observes that all have sinned and are consequently equally helpless and guilty, and that as God is no respecter of persons, all human creatures being equally his offspring and there being no reason why one should be preferred before another, his endless mercy has embraced all. The words for coming short he says have been variously translated, as failing to attain the glory of God, as not being able to bring glory to God, and as standing in need of the glory, that is the mercy, of God; the simple meaning seems to be that all have sinned and none can enjoy God’s glory but they that are holy, so that Jews and Gentiles alike have failed in their endeavours to attain it, since by the works of any law no human being can be justified. Wesley glosses the righteousness of God as the manner of becoming righteous which God has appointed, and the freedom from law as being without that previous obedience which the law requires, without reference to it or dependence on it; it is manifested in the gospel and attested by the Law itself and by the Prophets, that is by all the promises in the Old Testament. Of the doubled phrase he says the first refers to the Jews and the second to the Gentiles, and that there is no difference either as to the need of justification or as to the manner of it.

Barnes explains that the apostle, having shown the entire failure of all attempts to be justified by law whether among Jews or Gentiles, now states fully the plan of justification by Jesus Christ, which was the main design of the epistle. Without the law he takes to mean in a way different from personal obedience to the law, not that God abandoned his law, nor that Jesus Christ did not regard it, since he came to magnify it, nor that sinners after they are justified have no regard to it, but simply that justification could not be accomplished by personal obedience to any law of Jew or Gentile. Being witnessed he takes as borne witness to, the doctrine being no new one but found in the Old Testament, a remark made with special reference to the Jews; by the law he understands, as commonly among the Jews, the five books of Moses, and says the apostle means the doctrine was found in those books and not in the ten commandments strictly so called, since it is not a part of law to declare justification except by perfect obedience, and he points to the case of Abraham. The prophets he takes generally for the remainder of the Old Testament, the phrase the law and the prophets comprehending the whole of it, and cites the passages by which the doctrine was shown from Habakkuk, Isaiah and the Psalms, adding that the general tenor of the Old Testament and the appointment of sacrifices taught that man was a sinner and could not be justified by obedience to the moral law. The explanation Paul offers, he says, makes it plain that the phrase righteousness of God does not refer to an attribute of God but to his plan of making men righteous, since an attribute of God is not produced by faith in Jesus Christ; the phrase by faith of Jesus Christ means by faith in Jesus Christ, as in the parallel expressions elsewhere, and this cannot mean that faith is the meritorious cause of salvation but that it is the instrument or means by which we become justified, the state of mind to which God has been pleased to promise justification. The two following phrases he judges designed to be emphatic, though why both are used is not very apparent and many have supposed no essential difference; if there be one, the first may denote that this plan has come to all men, Jews and Gentiles, being provided and offered without distinction, and the second may guard against the supposition that all would therefore be saved by the mere fact that the announcement had reached them, since the benefits must actually come upon them or be applied to them, and there may be a reference to a robe placed upon one to hide his nakedness. No difference he limits to the matter under discussion, not denying differences of talent, education or property but only any distinction in the way men must be justified. Come short he renders as being deficient in regard to, having failed to obtain, and glory as praise or approbation, a common sense of the word: they had sought to be justified by God and had failed, their works of the law not securing his approbation. Ellicott renders the opening words as in these latter days, the Apostle conceiving of the history of the world as divided into periods, the period of the Gospel succeeding that of the Law and the Apostle and his readers belonging to it; the righteousness he renders as a righteousness of God, that is bestowed by him and wrought out by him, the reference being to the root-conception of righteousness as at once the great object and condition of the Messianic kingdom. Without the law he takes as complete independence of any law, though borne witness to by the Law of Moses, the new system being one into which the idea of law does not enter; is manifested he renders as hath been and continues to be manifested, the initial moment being the appearance of Christ upon earth and the scheme then begun still evolving itself; and he notes that the Apostle does not lose sight of the preparatory function of the older dispensation and its radical affinity to the new. The faith he defines as having Christ for its object, and adds that faith in Paul’s writings implies an intense attachment and devotion, with an intellectual basis necessarily involving belief in the existence and attributes of the Person for whom it is entertained, but moral in its operation, a recasting of the whole emotional nature in accordance with that belief together with a consequent change in character and practice. The second half of the doubled phrase he reports to be wanting in the best manuscripts and to be omitted. Of the last clause he insists on the tense, strictly all sinned, the Apostle looking back upon an act done in past time under the old legal dispensation without immediate reference to the present, and then saying that the result of that act, as distinct from the act itself, continues on into the present, so that mankind in a body fall short of, miss, or fail to obtain the glory of God; and that glory he takes to be probably not the glory which will be inaugurated for the saints at the Second Coming, since that is future, but rather something capable of being conferred in the present, the glory which comes from the favour and approval of God. Robertson marks the emphatic logical transition and says Paul now proceeds carefully to show the nature of the God-kind of righteousness which stands manifested, the necessity of which he has shown in the preceding chapters; it is apart from law of any kind and all of grace, but it is not a new discovery on Paul’s part, being witnessed by the law and the prophets and made plain continuously by God himself. The genitive he takes as objective, faith in Jesus Christ and not the subjective faith of Jesus Christ, in spite of Haussleiter’s contention for that idea, and supports it from the parallel constructions elsewhere and from the added words about those who believe. The word for difference he notes is the one used of the difference of sounds in musical instruments, and observes that the Jew was first in privilege as in penalty, but that being set right with God is offered to both on the same terms.

Theodoret asks who can sufficiently admire the power of the apostle’s wisdom, who shows at once that the law had come to an end and that it consented to grace; and aptly does he say manifested, for it has now laid clearly before all the hidden mystery of the dispensation, while in this comparison between grace and the law, by proving that both the law and the prophets were witnesses to the former, he exhibits the greatness of its conquest over the latter. He observes that what had been put down before is here repeated so that what was wanting might be added, since having said that the righteousness of God is manifested, and then interrupted the sentence to speak of its character, it was necessary to resume the phrase and to show that it was by faith in the Lord Christ that all who desired enjoyed it, whether Jews or Greeks; the first of the doubled phrases he refers to the Jews and the second to the other nations, and this he says Paul goes on to set forth more clearly in denying any difference.

debates: Why the righteousness is called God’s: Calvin leaves it open between a righteousness which alone can stand before God and one which God in mercy confers, and declines to contend for either; Barnes rules out any reference to a divine attribute, since an attribute is not produced by faith in Christ, and takes it for God’s plan of making men righteous; Ellicott renders it a righteousness of God, wrought out and bestowed by him.

Whether the second half of the doubled phrase belongs to the text: Ellicott reports it wanting in the best manuscripts and would omit it; Wesley and Theodoret assign the two phrases to Jews and Gentiles respectively, Barnes reads the second as guarding against a merely offered salvation, and Calvin treats the repetition as amplification.

What glory is come short of: Ellicott rules out the future glory of the Second Coming in favour of something conferrable now, the favour and approval of God, which Barnes likewise takes as praise or approbation; Clarke lists three renderings before settling on the rule that none but the holy can enjoy that glory; Henry divides it three ways, glorifying God, glorying before him, and being glorified by him.
outliers: Calvin disputes Augustine’s reading of the righteousness of God as the grace of regeneration, arguing from Abraham that Paul excludes even the works which God produces in his own people, and sorts the causes of justification as mercy efficient, Christ meritorious, and the word with faith instrumental.

Gill goes further than the others in denying faith any causal role at all, refusing it even the instrumental place on God’s side and leaving it only the apprehending and receiving of a righteousness that is not its own.
Ellicott defines faith as an intense attachment resting on an intellectual basis but moral in operation, a recasting of the whole emotional nature with a consequent change of character and practice.
Robertson observes that the word for difference is the one used of distinguishing the notes of musical instruments, and rejects Haussleiter’s subjective reading of the genitive of faith.
themes: witnessed by the law and the prophets

24.pericope_label: Being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus: whom God hath set forth to be a propitiation through faith in his blood, to declare his righteousness for the remission of sins that are past, through the forbearance of God

schools.summary: Gill says the several causes of justification are here mentioned, the moving cause being the free grace of God, by which he means not the Gospel or what some call the terms of the Gospel and its constitution, nor the grace of God infused into the heart, but the free love and favour of God as it is in his heart, wonderfully displayed in the business of a sinner’s justification: in his resolving upon the justification of his chosen ones in Christ, in fixing on the method, in pre-ordaining Christ to be the ransom, in calling Christ to engage in it, in Christ’s engaging as a surety, in the Father’s sending him to bring in everlasting righteousness, in Christ’s coming to do it and the gracious manner in which he wrought it out, and in the Father’s acceptation, imputation and donation of it. The propitiation he says may design either Christ the propitiator, the author of peace and reconciliation, or the propitiatory sacrifice by which he is so, both in allusion to the mercy seat which was a type of him; the apostle uses the same word which the Septuagint often renders the mercy seat by, and Philo the Jew calls it by the same name and says it was a symbol of the propitious power of God. Christ is the propitiation to God for sin, which must be understood of his making satisfaction to divine justice for the sins of his people, which were imputed to him, so that the law and justice of God made demands on him for them, which he answered to satisfaction by his obedience and sacrifice; this, as it could not be done by any other nor in any other way, is expressed by reconciliation and atonement, whence God may be said to be pacified, though not as if he had ever ceased to love his people. Calvin explains that since there remains nothing for men, as to themselves, but to perish, being smitten by the just judgment of God, they are justified freely through his mercy, Christ coming to the aid of this misery and communicating himself to believers so that they find in him alone all those things in which they are wanting. There is perhaps no passage in the whole Scripture, he says, which illustrates in a more striking manner the efficacy of his righteousness, for it shows that God’s mercy is the efficient cause, that Christ with his blood is the meritorious cause, that the formal or instrumental cause is faith in the word, and that the final cause is the glory of the divine justice and goodness. The repetition of grace he takes as deliberate: it might have been enough to oppose grace to merits, but lest we should imagine a half kind of grace he affirms more strongly what he means by repeating, and claims for God’s mercy alone the whole glory of our righteousness, which the sophists divide into parts and mutilate that they may not be constrained to confess their own poverty. Christ by his obedience satisfied the Father’s justice, and by undertaking our cause liberated us from the tyranny of death by which we were held captive, our guilt being removed on account of the sacrifice he offered; and here, Calvin adds, is fully confuted the gloss of those who make righteousness a quality, for if we are counted righteous before God because we are redeemed by a price, we certainly derive from another what is not in us. The propitiation he takes to allude to the ancient propitiatory, the same thing being really exhibited in Christ which had been previously typified, so that we are not otherwise just than through Christ propitiating the Father for us. The verb he says means sometimes to determine beforehand and sometimes to set forth: if the first, Paul refers to the gratuitous mercy of God in having appointed Christ as our Mediator that he might appease the Father by the sacrifice of his death, and it is no small commendation of God’s grace that of his own good will he sought out a way by which he might remove our curse; but since the other view cannot be disproved, Calvin will not undertake to decide the question, and rests on what Paul especially meant, that God without having regard to Christ is always angry with us and that we are reconciled to him when we are accepted through his righteousness — God not hating in us his own workmanship, that is as we are formed men, but hating our uncleanness, which has extinguished the light of his image, and loving and embracing us as his own pure workmanship when the washing of Christ has cleansed it away.

Clarke says that so far from being able to attain the glory of God by their obedience they are all guilty, and to be saved must be freely pardoned by God’s grace, which is shown to them who believe through the ransom price that is in the sacrifice of Christ Jesus. The word he analyses as compounded of the preposition and the verb to redeem, properly meaning the price laid down for the redemption of a captive, and he cites Rosenmüller that this redemption comprehends whatsoever Christ taught, did or suffered in order to free men from evil and especially from sin, the source of evils; that it here means the liberation purchased by the blood-shedding of Christ he shows from the parallel passages where redemption through his blood is the forgiveness of sins. He adds Suidas, who defines the noun as a reward or the price given to be redeemed from the slavery of the barbarians, and Schleusner, who says no man can deny that the word properly denotes the redemption of one held captive, whether taken in war or otherwise, procured by the payment of a price; that the word also means any deliverance where no price is paid nobody will dispute, but that it means redemption by a price laid down, and the redemption of the soul by the price of the death of Christ, he holds the scriptures sufficiently prove. The propitiation he takes for the mercy-seat or place of atonement, because the blood of the sacrifice was sprinkled on and before it in order to obtain remission, the mercy-seat being the lid or cover of the ark where God was manifest between the cherubim, so that the atonement made in this place was properly made to God himself; and both this and the redemption he refers to the sacrificial death of Christ as the atonement made and the price paid down. The declaration of righteousness he renders as the manifestation of it, God’s mercy in saving sinners by sending Christ to make an atonement, thereby declaring his readiness to remit all past transgressions committed by Jews and Gentiles alike during the time in which his merciful forbearance was exercised toward the world, which he applies also to all who hear the Gospel now. Wesley glosses being justified as pardoned and accepted, freely as without any merit of their own, by his grace as not by their own righteousness or works, and through the redemption as the price Christ has paid. One of these expressions, he says, might have served to convey the apostle’s meaning, but he doubles his assertion in order to give us the fullest conviction of the truth and to impress us with a sense of its peculiar importance, since it is not possible to find words that should more absolutely exclude all consideration of our own works and obedience, or more emphatically ascribe the whole of our justification to free, unmerited goodness. The setting forth he takes to be before angels and men, and the propitiation to appease an offended God, adding sharply that if, as some teach, God never was offended, there was no need of this propitiation, and if so, Christ died in vain. The declaration of righteousness he takes to demonstrate not only God’s clemency but his justice, even that vindictive justice whose essential character and principal office is to punish sin; and the remission of past sins he limits to all the sins antecedent to their believing.

Barnes explains being justified as being treated as if righteous, that is regarded and treated as if they had kept the law, which could not be by any merit of their own and must therefore be by mere favour and as a matter not of right but of gift. Freely he takes as standing opposed to what is purchased or obtained by labour or claimed as a right, an undeserved gift not merited by obedience to the law; it does not mean that it was obtained without any price from any one, since the Lord Jesus purchased it with his own blood and to him it becomes a matter of justice that those given to him should be justified, but to us it is entirely a matter of gift. The word for redemption he traces to a root properly denoting the price paid for a prisoner of war, the ransom or stipulated purchase-money which being paid the captive is set free, and though the word is sometimes used broadly of deliverance by any means without reference to a price, that is not the sense here, since the apostle proceeds in the next verse to specify the price by which the redemption was effected. The verb of setting forth he says properly means to place in public view, to exhibit in a conspicuous situation, as goods are exposed for sale or as prizes were displayed at the Greek games; it sometimes means decreeing or purposing, and many have supposed that to be the sense here, but the connexion seems to require the usual signification, so that God has publicly exhibited Christ as a propitiatory sacrifice, the exhibition being made by his being offered on the cross in the face of angels and of men, not concealed but done openly. The word for propitiation he says occurs in only one other place in the New Testament, of the lid or cover of the ark, and is often used in that sense by the Greek Old Testament, the Hebrew name coming from a verb meaning to cover; it was from that place that God was represented as speaking to Israel and as pronouncing pardon, the blood of the great day of atonement being sprinkled upon and before it. Why the name is given to Christ he examines carefully: it cannot apply in any literal sense, and the analogy between the golden cover and the Lord Jesus must be very slight, but he notes five correspondences, that the main idea in both is God’s being reconciled to his people, that the reconciliation was in both cases effected by blood, that in both it was blood of atonement though here Christ’s own, that in both there was a sacrifice, and that in both a sacrifice for sin was joined to the idea. Hence the main idea is to set forth Christ as a sacrifice for sin, the word being an adjective which may be joined to the noun sacrifice as well as used of the covering of the ark, a meaning which also accords with its classical use of a propitiatory offering; Christ is thus represented not as a mercy-seat, which would be unintelligible, but as the medium and expiation by which reconciliation is produced. Through faith he renders as by means of faith, since the offering has been made but will not be applied except where there is faith. On the blood he explains that among the Jews blood was regarded as the seat of life, whence they were commanded not to eat it and the efficacy of their sacrifices was supposed to consist in it; the same opinion, he adds, has been held by not a few celebrated physiologists ancient and modern, and he cites Homer’s purple death and Virgil’s purple life, Empedocles and Critias among the Greeks, and Harvey, Hoffman, Huxham and John Hunter among the moderns. When the blood of Christ is spoken of in the New Testament, therefore, it means the offering of his life as a sacrifice. To declare he renders as for the purpose of showing or exhibiting, and his righteousness he refuses to take of an attribute, whether veracity, holiness, goodness or essential justice as most interpreters have done, holding that the whole connexion requires his plan of justifying sinners. The word for remission, he notes, occurs nowhere else in the New Testament nor in the Greek Old Testament, and means passing by as not noticing and hence forgiving; the sins that are past he refers not to former generations, as has commonly been supposed, but to the past lives of the individuals who are justified, since the scope of the passage is not an historical fact but the way in which sin is to be forgiven under the gospel, and since on the other reading it would not be easy to avoid the doctrine of universal salvation. The forbearance of God he explains as his long-suffering, in that he did not come forth in judgment when the sin was committed but spared men though deserving punishment; and he closes by transcribing the poet Cowper’s account of his own conversion, which he dates from reading this very verse in his melancholy at St Alban’s. Ellicott says we should more naturally say but now are justified, the Greek construction being peculiar and admitting two accounts, either that the participle corresponds to the earlier phrase about all them that believe with an irregularity of case suggested by the preceding sentence, or that the construction is regular and the participle dependent on the last finite verb, so that they come short of the glory of God and in that very state of destitution are justified. Freely he renders gratuitously, without exertion or merit on their part; the means by which justification is wrought out is the death and atonement of Christ, its ulterior cause the grace of God. Redemption he renders literally as ransoming, and says the notion contains in itself the triple idea of a bondage, a deliverance, and the payment of an equivalent as the means of that deliverance: the bondage is the state of sin and guilt with the expectation of punishment, the deliverance is the removal of that state and the opening of a prospect of eternal happiness, and the equivalent paid by Christ is the shedding of his own blood, which is the pivot on which the whole idea of redemption turns. It is therefore clear, he argues, that the redemption of the sinner is an act wrought objectively and in the first instance independently of any change of condition in him, and cannot be explained as a purely subjective process wrought in the sinner through the influence of Christ’s death; there is implied not only a change in the recipient of the atonement but a change wrought without his co-operation in the relations between God and man, something in the death of Christ which determines the will of God as well as something which acts upon the will of man. This element he holds too essential a part of the metaphor and too clearly established by parallel metaphors to be explained away, though what the terms propitiation and equivalent can mean as applied to God we do not know and it perhaps does not become us too curiously to inquire; and he notes that the doctrine so stated is not peculiar to Paul nor original with him, being found in the Synoptic Gospels and in Hebrews. The verb he renders as set forth, publicly exhibited, in the single act of the death upon the cross, and the noun as properly meaning that which renders propitious, here that which renders God propitious, since in some way not explained in this passage the death of Christ did act so as to render God propitious toward men. He records the remarkable use of the same Greek word in the Greek Old Testament for the mercy-seat and the view that Christ is the mercy-seat of the New Covenant, and answers that it would hardly be a conclusive objection that Christ would then be at once the victim whose blood is sprinkled and the covering on which it is sprinkled, since a similar double reference occurs in Hebrews; on the whole, however, he finds reasons for supplying rather the idea of sacrifice, as more entirely in keeping with the context and especially supported by the public setting forth, whereas the ark was confined to the secrecy of the Holy of Holies, and by the phrase in his blood. Faith he calls the apprehending cause by which the proffered pardon takes effect upon the soul of the believer; and the words about the blood he thinks best not joined with faith but referred to the main verb, so that God set Christ forth by the shedding of his blood to be a propitiatory offering through faith, since it was in the shedding of the blood that the essence of the atonement consisted. Robertson parses the participle as a present passive of repeated action, each being set right, and calls grace the wonderful word which so richly expresses Paul’s idea of salvation as God’s free gift. Redemption he explains as a releasing by ransom, notes that we have the words of Jesus that he came to give his life a ransom for many, and adds that the noun is common in the papyri as the purchase-money in freeing slaves, so that God did not set men right out of hand with nothing done about men’s sins. The verb of setting forth he parses as a second aorist middle, God setting before himself and doing it publicly before the whole world. Of the propitiation he says the only other New Testament example is the overshadowed mercy seat in Hebrews, where the adjective is used as a substantive for the propitiatory place, but that this idea does not suit here; Deissmann has produced examples from inscriptions where it is used as an adjective meaning a votive offering or propitiatory gift, and concludes of this verse that the crucified Christ is the votive gift of the divine love for the salvation of men, so that there is no longer room for doubting its meaning. The words about the blood he connects with the setting forth rather than with faith.

Theodoret says that by bringing faith alone we have received remission of our sins, in that the Lord Christ has offered up his own body for us to be, as it were, the price of redemption. The propitiatory he describes as a golden plate which lay over the ark, having at either end the figure of a cherub, from which the mercy of God was manifested to the high priest in his ministrations; and he teaches that the Lord Christ was the true propitiatory, that ancient one being but a type of this. The name, however, he applies to Christ as man and not as God, for as God he himself speaks from the propitiatory, while as man he receives this appellation even as he receives others, such as sheep and lamb and sin and curse and the like. Of the closing clauses he says that God has both exhibited his own mercy in so long bearing with sinners and made manifest his righteousness to all men, for that it was not without any further view that he thus bore with sinners, but as preparing for them this means of salvation, as the next sentence shows.

debates: Whether the word means the mercy-seat or a propitiatory sacrifice: Gill and Clarke take the mercy-seat allusion, and Theodoret with them, though he restricts the title to Christ as man, since as God he is the one who speaks from the propitiatory; Barnes works through five correspondences with the ark and then rejects the identification, since Christ as a mercy-seat would be unintelligible; Ellicott weighs both and prefers sacrifice, because a public setting forth suits ill with a thing hidden in the Holy of Holies; Robertson rejects the mercy-seat outright and, following the inscriptions, makes it a votive or propitiatory gift.

Whether the verb means fore-ordained or publicly exhibited: Barnes allows that many have taken the first sense but holds the connexion to require the second, the exhibition being made on the cross in the face of angels and men; Calvin sets out what would follow from each and expressly declines to decide the question.

What the sins passed over are: Barnes confines them to the past lives of the individuals justified and warns that referring them to former generations makes the doctrine of universal salvation hard to avoid; Wesley limits them to all the sins antecedent to believing; Clarke extends them to whatever Jews and Gentiles committed during the time of God’s forbearance.
outliers: Barnes transcribes the poet Cowper’s account of his own conversion, which Cowper dated from opening a Bible in his melancholy and reading this very verse.
Barnes supports the Hebrew view of blood as the seat of life from Homer and Virgil and from Empedocles and Critias, and then from Harvey, Hoffman, Huxham and John Hunter among the moderns.
Ellicott grants that what the terms propitiation and equivalent can mean as applied to God we do not know, and that it perhaps does not become us too curiously to inquire.
Wesley adds that if, as some teach, God never was offended, there was no need of this propitiation, and if so, Christ died in vain.
themes: remission of sins that are past

26.pericope_label: To declare, I say, at this time his righteousness: that he might be just, and the justifier of him which believeth in Jesus. Where is boasting then? It is excluded. By what law? of works? Nay: but by the law of faith. Therefore we conclude that a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law

schools.summary: Gill takes the end to be further explained as declaring the righteousness of God at this time, under the Gospel dispensation, in which there was such a display of the grace, mercy and goodness of God. Of the boasting he says there is no room nor reason for it, either in Jews or Gentiles: not in the Jews, who were very apt to boast of being Abraham’s seed, of their circumcision, of being Israelites, of having and keeping the law, of God being their God and of their knowledge of him; nor in the Gentiles, who were ready to boast of their philosophy, wisdom and learning, of their self-sufficiency and freewill and of the things they had in their own power. The last verse he calls the conclusion from the premises, the sum total of the whole account. Calvin observes that what had been true at all times is here applied to the time when Christ was revealed, and not without reason, for what was formerly known in an obscure manner under shadows God openly manifested in his Son, so that the coming of Christ was the time of his good pleasure and the day of salvation; God had indeed in all ages given some evidence of his righteousness, but it appeared far brighter when the sun of righteousness shone, and the comparison between the Old and the New Testament ought to be noticed, since only then was the righteousness of God revealed. That righteousness he defines as consisting of two parts: the first, that God is just, not as one among many but as one who contains within himself all fulness of righteousness, since complete and full praise such as is due is not otherwise given to him but when he alone obtains the name and the honour of being just while the whole human race is condemned for injustice; and the second, the communication of righteousness, since God by no means keeps his riches laid up in himself but pours them forth upon men, so that his righteousness shines in us whenever he justifies us by faith in Christ, for in vain were Christ given us for righteousness unless there were the fruition of him by faith. It hence follows that all were unjust and lost in themselves until a remedy from heaven was offered them. Of the exclusion of boasting he says that the Apostle, having with reasons abundantly strong cast men down from their confidence in works, now triumphs over their folly, and that this exulting conclusion was necessary, for on this subject to teach us would not have been enough but it was necessary that the Holy Spirit should loudly thunder in order to lay prostrate our loftiness. Glorying is beyond all doubt excluded, since we cannot adduce anything of our own worthy of being approved by God; and if the material of glorying be merit, whether of congruity or of condignity, by which man would conciliate God, both are here annihilated, for Paul treats not of the lessening or modifying of merit but leaves not a particle behind. To the question in what sense the Apostle denies that our merits are excluded by the law, having before proved that we are condemned by the law, he answers that Paul means here that were righteousness to be had by the law of works our glorying would not be excluded, but as it is by faith alone there is nothing that we can claim for ourselves, since faith receives all from God and brings nothing except an humble confession of want; and the contrast between faith and works ought to be carefully noticed, works being mentioned without any limitation, so that he speaks neither of ceremonies only nor of any external work specifically but includes all the merits of works that can possibly be imagined. The name of law he grants is here given to faith with no strict correctness, but says this by no means obscures the meaning, since what he understands is that when we come to the rule of faith the whole glorying in works is laid prostrate, as though he said that the righteousness of works is commended by the law but that of faith has its own law, which leaves to works, whatever they may be, no righteousness. The last verse he calls the main proposition, drawn as one that is incontrovertible, and notes that in nothing do our adversaries labour more than in attempts to blend faith with the merits of works, allowing that man is justified by faith but not by faith alone and placing the efficacy of justification in love while in words ascribing it to faith; but Paul affirms justification to be so gratuitous that it can by no means be associated with the merit of works. Why he names the works of the law Calvin has already explained, and holds it quite absurd to confine them to ceremonies and frigid also the gloss that works are those which are outward and done without the Spirit of Christ, since the added word means the same as though he called them meritorious, what is referred to being the reward promised in the law. What James says, that man is not justified by faith alone but also by works, he holds not to militate against this view at all, the reconciling of the two depending chiefly on the drift of the argument James pursues, whose question is not how men attain righteousness before God but how they prove to others that they are justified, his object being to confute hypocrites who vainly boasted that they had faith; gross then is the sophistry which will not admit that the word justify is taken in a different sense by James from that in which Paul uses it, since they handle different subjects, and James meant no more than that man is not made or proved to be just by a feigned or dead faith and must prove his righteousness by his works.

Henry says God will have the great work of the justification and salvation of sinners carried on from first to last so as to shut out boasting, since if we were saved by our own works boasting would not be excluded, whereas the way of justification by faith for ever shuts it out. Yet believers are not left to be lawless: faith is a law, and it is a working grace wherever it is in truth; by faith, which in this matter is not an act of obedience or a good work but the forming of the relation between Christ and the sinner, it becomes proper that the believer should be pardoned and justified for the sake of the Saviour, and that the unbeliever who is not thus united to him should remain under condemnation. The law, he adds, is still of use to convince us of what is past and to direct us for the future, and though we cannot be saved by it as a covenant we own and submit to it as a rule in the hand of the Mediator.

Clarke says the declaration is a manifesting now, by the dispensation of the Gospel, of God’s righteousness and infinite mercy, and in such a way that he might still appear to be the just God and yet the justifier and pardoner of him who believes in Jesus; here we learn that God designed to give the most evident displays both of his justice and of his mercy, of his justice in requiring a sacrifice and absolutely refusing to give salvation to a lost world in any other way, and of his mercy in providing the sacrifice which his justice required, so that because Jesus was an atonement and a ransom price for the sin of the world, God can consistently with his justice pardon every soul that believes in him. This he calls the full discovery of God’s righteousness, of his wonderful method of magnifying his law and making it honourable, of showing the infinite purity of his justice and of saving a lost world. He then resumes his dialogue: the Jew, finding his boasted privileges at stake, interrupts and asks where the glorying is, whether there is nothing in which they can trust for acceptance, no merit of their own, nothing accruing from circumcision and the covenant; the Apostle answers that it is shut out, the door of heaven being shut against everything of this kind. The Jew asks by what rule or doctrine it is shut out, whether by the law of works, the rule of obedience God gave; and the Apostle answers, not by the law of works, since glorying is not cut off by that, which stands in full force as the rule of life, but the law of works grants no pardon, requiring obedience and threatening the disobedient with death, so that all glorying in the expectation of salvation through one’s own obedience is excluded by the doctrine of faith, faith alone in the mercy of God through the propitiation made by the blood of Jesus being that by which a man can be justified and taken into the divine favour. The conclusion he paraphrases as the fair rational consequence drawn by the apostles and Christian teachers, that any man has his sins blotted out and is received into the divine favour by faith in Christ’s blood, without the deeds of the law, which never could afford either to Jew or Gentile a ground of justification, since both have sinned against the law God gave them and consequently forfeited all right and title to the blessings the obedient might claim. Wesley takes the demonstration to be of both God’s justice and his mercy, showing his justice on his own Son and yet being the merciful justifier of every one that believes; the attribute of justice must be preserved inviolate, and inviolate it is preserved if there was a real infliction of punishment on our Saviour, so that on this plan all the attributes harmonise, every attribute being glorified and not one superseded, no, nor so much as clouded. The exclusion he refers to the boasting of the Jew against the Gentile, and denies that it is excluded by the law of works, which would have left room for boasting, but by the law of faith, since this requires all without distinction to apply as guilty and helpless sinners to the free mercy of God in Christ; the law of faith he defines as that divine constitution which makes faith, not works, the condition of acceptance. Of the conclusion he adds the exact qualification, that a man is justified by faith and even by this not as it is a work but as it receives Christ, and consequently has something essentially different from all our works whatsoever.

Barnes says this verse contains the substance of the gospel, and that just here does not mean benevolent or merciful but refers to God’s having retained the integrity of his character as a moral Governor, showing a due regard to his law and to its penalty by his plan of salvation; should he forgive sinners without an atonement, justice would be sacrificed and abandoned, the law would cease to have terrors for the guilty and its penalty would be a nullity. In the plan of salvation he has shown a regard to the law by appointing his Son to be a substitute in the place of sinners, not to endure its precise penalty, since his sufferings were not eternal nor attended with remorse of conscience or with despair, which are the proper penalty of the law, but to endure so much as to accomplish the same ends as if those who shall be saved had been doomed to eternal death; thus he showed that the law could not be violated without introducing suffering and could not be broken with impunity, and secured the proper honour to his character as a lover of his law, a hater of sin and a just God. When an executive pardons offenders, he adds, there is an abandonment of the principles of justice and law, the sentence being set aside and the threatening departed from without compensation; but not so with God, who shows no less regard to his law in pardoning than in punishing, and this is the grand and peculiar feature of the gospel plan. Where boasting is concerned he takes the word law in the sense of arrangement, rule or economy, and argues that if the law which commands works had justified them they would have had ground of self-confidence, but a plan which led to boasting and self-satisfaction and pride could not be true; the law of faith is the rule which proclaims that we have no merit, that we are lost sinners and are to be justified only by faith. The conclusion he takes as the result of the previous train of argument, that all who are justified are so by believing and that there is no other way, without works as a meritorious ground; he notes that Luther often called this doctrine the article on which the church stood or fell, and says it is so, since if this doctrine is held entire all others will be held with it and if it is abandoned all others will fall also. He remarks, however, that the doctrine by no means interferes with the doctrine that good works are to be performed by Christians, Paul urging this as much as any writer in the New Testament, his point being only that they are not to be relied on as a ground of justification. Ellicott says the second object of the death of Christ was to remove the misconceptions that might be caused by the apparent condoning of sins committed in times anterior to the Christian revelation, a special word being used to indicate that these sins were not wiped away and dismissed altogether but rather passed over or overlooked, which was due to the forbearance of God, who as it were suspended the execution of his vengeance; now the Apostle shows by the death of Christ that justice which had apparently slept was vindicated. Thus God appeared in a double character, at once as just or righteous himself and as producing a state of righteousness in the believer: under the Old Testament God had been revealed as just, but the justice or righteousness of God was not met by any corresponding righteousness on the part of man and therefore could only issue in condemnation, whereas under the New Testament the justice of God remained the same but was met by a corresponding state of righteousness in the believer, a righteousness however not inherent but superinduced by God himself through the process of justification by faith, so that the great Messianic condition of righteousness was fulfilled. The exclusion he renders strictly as it was excluded, at the moment when the law of faith, that is the gospel, was brought in; and the following question he renders properly as by what kind of law, whether one which calls for works or one that calls for faith, the law of faith being another name for the gospel. In the last verse he reports a remarkable division of some of the best authorities between therefore and for, the weight of authority seeming somewhat in favour of for, which also makes the best sense, since that boasting is excluded is much rather the consequence than the cause of the principle that man is justified by faith, a principle the Apostle regards as sufficiently proved by his previous argument; and he objects that the English conveys too much the idea of an inference, the statement being rather made in the form of an assertion, we consider or we hold that a man, any human being whether Jew or Greek, is justified by faith independently of any works prescribed by law. Robertson notes that the preposition of the first clause is changed from that of the preceding verse while the point is repeated, and renders the time as in the now crisis, in contrast with what was done aforetime. The double title he calls the key phrase which establishes the connexion between the righteousness of God and the righteousness which is by faith, and says that nowhere has Paul put the problem of God more acutely or profoundly, since to pronounce the unrighteous righteous is unjust by itself, while God’s mercy would not allow him to leave man to his fate and God’s justice demanded some punishment for sin, the only possible way to save some being the propitiatory offering of Christ and the call for faith on man’s part. The exclusion he parses as a first aorist effective passive, it is completely shut out, glorying being on man’s part, and takes the law of faith as the principle of faith in harmony with God’s love and grace. The final verb he parses as a present middle meaning that this is his fixed opinion, notes the variant reading of the connecting particle, and observes that Paul is restating what he had said a few verses earlier.

Theodoret says the question about boasting must be read interrogatively, and then comes the answer that it is excluded; the Apostle says not destroyed but excluded, that is, that it has no longer any place. By boasting he means the haughty self-esteem of the Jews, who exalted themselves as the only possessors of God’s favour, whereas now, divine grace having appeared abroad and been shed among all nations, this arrogance had been put out of the question, in that God had given to man a short and easy means of salvation in faith. He calls faith here a law, Theodoret adds, not from inconsideration but as recollecting the prophecy of Jeremiah that in those days the Lord would make a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah, not according to the covenant that he made with their fathers. Of the conclusion he observes that by law here the Apostle means that of Moses, but that he says not we conclude that by faith a Jew is justified but a man, the common name of the whole human race.

debates: Whether the substitute bore the precise penalty: Barnes denies it, since Christ’s sufferings were neither eternal nor attended with remorse or despair, and says only that they accomplished the same ends; Wesley holds that justice is kept inviolate only if there was a real infliction of punishment on the Saviour; Robertson states the difficulty rather than resolving it, that pronouncing the unrighteous righteous is by itself unjust while mercy would not leave man to his fate.
