How faith can be called a law: Calvin grants that the name is given without strict correctness, and explains that the righteousness of faith has a law of its own which leaves works no righteousness; Theodoret defends the usage from Jeremiah’s prophecy of a covenant not according to the one made with the fathers; Barnes takes law here for an arrangement or economy, and Wesley for the divine constitution which makes faith the condition of acceptance.

How the last sentence opens: Ellicott reports the best authorities divided between therefore and for, prefers for as making the better sense since the exclusion of boasting is the consequence rather than the cause, and objects that we conclude suggests an inference where the Greek asserts; Robertson notes the same variant; Clarke keeps the inference and calls it a proof by fair rational consequence.
outliers: Barnes contrasts the divine pardon with an executive’s, which sets the sentence aside without compensation and so abandons the principles of justice, and recalls Luther’s calling this the article by which the church stands or falls.

Calvin says that teaching would not have been enough on this head and that the Holy Spirit had to thunder in order to lay our loftiness prostrate, merit of congruity and of condignity alike being annihilated rather than reduced.

Calvin reconciles the apparent conflict with James by distinguishing the questions, since James asks not how men attain righteousness before God but how they prove it to others, and was confuting hypocrites who boasted of a dead faith.
Gill inventories what the exclusion costs each side, the Jew his descent and circumcision and law, the Gentile his philosophy and self-sufficiency and freewill.

29.pericope_label: Is he the God of the Jews only? is he not also of the Gentiles? Yes, of the Gentiles also: seeing it is one God, which shall justify the circumcision by faith, and uncircumcision through faith. Do we then make void the law through faith? God forbid: yea, we establish the law

schools.summary: Gill says the Jews made their boast of God as theirs only and would not allow the Gentiles any interest in him. On the unity he observes that God is one in nature and essence, though there are three persons in the Godhead, whence it appears that he who is the God of the Jews is also the God of the Gentiles, or there would be more gods than one; and that these are justified in one and the same manner, or God must be divided, for as he is one in nature so he is one in will, in his promises and in the methods of his grace. The closing question he says is answered by way of detestation. Calvin calls this the second proposition, that this righteousness belongs no more to the Jews than to the Gentiles, and a great matter to be urged, in order that a free passage might be made for the kingdom of Christ through the whole world. Paul does not ask simply whether God was the Creator of the Gentiles, which was admitted without any dispute, but whether he designed to manifest himself as a Saviour also to them; and as he had put all mankind on a level and brought them to the same condition, any difference between them is from God and not from themselves. If it be true that God designs to make all the nations of the earth partakers of his mercy, then salvation, and the righteousness necessary for salvation, must be extended to all; and under the name of God as theirs is conveyed an intimation of a mutual relationship often mentioned in Scripture, that he will be to them a God and they shall be to him a people, since the circumstance that God for a time chose for himself a peculiar people did not make void the origin of mankind, who were all formed after the image of God and were to be brought up in the hope of a blessed eternity. The future tense he takes for the present after the manner of the Hebrew language, though some consider that the day of judgment is referred to. In saying that some are justified by faith and some through faith, Paul seems to Calvin to have indulged himself in varying his language while expressing the same thing, and for this end, that he might touch on the folly of the Jews, who imagined a difference between themselves and the Gentiles though on the subject of justification there was no difference whatever; for since men become partakers of this grace by faith only, and since faith in all is the same, it is absurd to make a distinction in what is so much alike. He is hence led to think that there is something ironical in the words, as though Paul said that if any wishes to have a difference made between the Gentile and the Jew, let him take this, that the one obtains righteousness by faith and the other through faith; but it may be, he allows, that some will prefer the distinction that the Jews were justified by faith because they were born the heirs of grace, the right of adoption being transmitted to them from the fathers, and that the Gentiles were justified through faith because the covenant to them was adventitious. On the last verse he explains why the objection arises: when the law is opposed to faith the flesh immediately suspects that there is some contrariety, as though the one were adverse to the other, and this false notion prevails especially among those imbued with wrong ideas as to the law, who leave the promises and seek nothing else through it but the righteousness of works; on this account not only Paul but our Lord himself was evil spoken of by the Jews, as though in all his preaching he aimed at the abrogation of the law, whence he made the protest that he came not to undo but to fulfil it. The suspicion regards the moral as well as the ceremonial law, since as the gospel has put an end to the Mosaic ceremonies it is supposed to tend to destroy the whole dispensation of Moses, and as it sweeps away all the righteousness of works it is believed to be opposed to those testimonies of the law by which the Lord declared that he had prescribed the way of righteousness; Calvin therefore takes the defence not only as to ceremonies, nor as to the commandments called moral, but with regard to the whole law universally. The law is in reality confirmed and established through faith in Christ, he argues, inasmuch as it was given for this end, to lead man to Christ by showing him his iniquity; without this it cannot be fulfilled and in vain will it require what ought to be done, nor can it do anything but irritate lust and increase man’s condemnation, but where there is a coming to Christ there is first found in him the perfect righteousness of the law, which becomes ours by imputation, and then sanctification, by which our hearts are prepared to keep the law, imperfectly indeed but with an aiming at the work. Similar is the case with the ceremonies, which cease and vanish away when Christ comes but are in reality confirmed by him, since viewed in themselves they are vain and shadowy images and attain something real and solid only when their end is regarded, their chief confirmation consisting in their accomplishment in Christ. Let us then bear in mind, he concludes, so to dispense the gospel that by our mode of teaching the law may be confirmed, but let it be sustained by no other strength than that of faith in Christ.

Clarke warns the Jew not to begin to suppose that because he cannot be justified by the works of the law, and God has in mercy found out a new method of saving him, this mercy shall apply to the Jews exclusively; God is the maker, preserver and redeemer of the Gentiles also, as much as of the Jews, since all have equally sinned and there is no reason, if God be disposed to show mercy at all, that he should prefer the one to the other, all being equally guilty, sinful and necessitous. The unity he renders as the apostle’s meaning that it is one and the same God who made both Jews and Gentiles, who shall pardon the believing Jews by faith and the believing Gentiles by the same faith, since there is but one Saviour and one atonement provided for the whole. It is fanciful, he says, to suppose that the apostle has one meaning by the first preposition and a different meaning by the second; both are to be understood in precisely the same sense, only the addition of the article in the second case extends and more pointedly ascertains the meaning, so that it is one and the same God who shall justify the believing Jews by faith and the believing Gentiles by that same faith. On the last verse he distinguishes two senses of law: by law we may understand the whole of the Mosaic law in its rites and ceremonies, of which Christ was the subject and the end, since all that law had respect to him, and the doctrine of faith established its very claims and demands by showing that all was accomplished in the passion and death of Christ, for without shedding of blood the law would allow no remission; and we may understand also the moral law, which relates to the regulation of the conduct of men, and this law also was established by the doctrine of salvation by faith, because this faith works by love and love is the principle of obedience, so that whoever receives salvation through faith in Christ receives power to live in holy obedience to every moral precept. Reviewing the chapter he says he has followed Dr Taylor’s plan and especially its dialogue form but has often differed from him, since Taylor cannot allow the death of Christ to be considered as a price paid down for the salvation of men, whereas Clarke cannot understand the apostle in any other way nor see the force of his conclusions on any other ground than that the passion and death of Christ were an atonement made to divine justice on man’s behalf. The chapter he calls a fine and striking synopsis of the whole Christian system, the wretched state of man being exhibited in one section and the plan of salvation in another, which a pious writer calls the Catechism of Christian Righteousness; and he sets out that catechism in a series of questions and answers on how God is glorified in us, what his grace works, by whom salvation is given, what price was paid, what the blood effects, how it is applied, and for whom it is designed. He warns finally against Antinomianism, that is against supposing that because Christ has been obedient unto death there is no necessity for our obedience to his righteous commandments, since if this were so the grace of Christ would tend to the destruction of the law and not to its establishment; he only is saved from his sins who has the law of God written in his heart, and he alone has it written there who lives an innocent, holy and useful life. Wesley answers the first question briefly, that God is surely the God of the Gentiles also, as both nature and the scriptures show; and of the last verse he says that we establish both the authority, the purity and the end of the law, by defending that which the law attests, by pointing out Christ, the end of it, and by showing how it may be fulfilled in its purity.

Barnes explains that the Jews supposed God to be the God of their nation only and that they alone were to be admitted to his favour, whereas since all alike had sinned and the plan of salvation by faith was adapted to sinners without any special reference to Jews, God could show favours to all and all might be admitted on the same terms. The oneness he takes to mean the same God, there being but one, whose plan is equally fitted to Jew and Gentile; the circumcision he glosses as the Jews and the uncircumcision as all who were not Jews, and he holds there is no difference in the meaning of the two phrases about faith, both denoting that faith is the instrumental cause of justification. The final objection he states in its usual form, that the doctrine of justification by faith tends to licentiousness, an objection naturally made and since made thousands of times; the word law he understands of the moral law and not merely of the Old Testament, as is evident from the earlier verses where no man could be justified by conformity with the moral law. The denial he makes explicit, and shows how the law is established in three ways: God showed respect to it in being unwilling to pardon sinners without an atonement, proving that it could not be violated with impunity and that he was resolved to fulfil its threatenings; Jesus Christ came to magnify it and make it honourable, showing respect to it in his life and dying to show that God was determined to inflict its penalty; and the plan of justification by faith leads to an observance of the law, since the sinner sees the evil of transgression and the respect God has shown to the law, gives his heart to God and yields himself to obey. All the sentiments arising from conviction of sin, from gratitude and from love to God prompt him to obedience, and the fact that Christ endured such sufferings to show the evil of violating the law is one of the strongest motives, since we do not easily repeat that which overwhelms our best friends in calamity and are brought to hate what inflicted such woes on the Saviour’s soul; Barnes quotes some verses of Watts to the same effect and calls this an advantage in moral influence which no cold abstract law ever has over the human mind, one of the chief glories of the plan of salvation being that while it justifies the sinner it brings a new set of influences from heaven to produce obedience. Ellicott would insert an alternative particle in the first question and paraphrases it as asking whether we are to suppose that God belongs to the Jews only, taking up the point of the previous verse that any man simply as man and without regard to distinction of race was capable of justification. The next clause he renders with a slight change of reading as if at least, if, as we are sure is the case, and calls the argument strictly logical: if there is to be any distinction between Jew and Gentile, this can only be on the assumption either that there are more gods than one by whom they will be justified, or that they will be justified by some different law in some different way; but neither of these is the case, and therefore no distinction follows. The future he takes to signify throughout the Christian dispensation, wherever the Christian system extends. Of the two prepositional phrases he says that in the one case faith is regarded as the instrument and in the other as the means, but that the two expressions come to be almost convertible; nor is any essential difference indicated by the fact that the first noun has not the article while the second has it, the former being more abstract, the quality of faith in man, and the latter more concrete, faith as embodied in the gospel, the two English prepositions differing no more than instrument and means. The closing question he thinks right, in opposition to many commentators, to take as an isolated statement to be worked out more fully afterwards, since it cannot without straining be connected directly with what follows; the Apostle deals with two objections to his theory of justification by faith, that there ought to be a different rule for the Jew and for the Gentile, and that if not, the law is practically abolished, and he meets the latter by a contradiction, saying that it is not abolished but confirmed. This, however, Ellicott adds, is drawing upon the stock of conclusions in Paul’s own mind to which he had come by process of meditation, the detailed proof being reserved. Robertson remarks of the Gentiles that the Jews overlooked this then and some Christians do now. The opening particle of the next verse he takes in the correct text to mean if on the whole, a species of rhetorical politeness used of that about which there is no doubt; the first phrase about faith he renders as out of faith, springing out of, and the second as by means of the faith just mentioned, the one preposition denoting source and the other intermediate agency or attendant circumstance. The final verb he parses as a present indicative active of a late form, notes that Paul had hinted at this earlier, and says he will show how in the following chapter, where Abraham himself is an example of faith and in his life illustrates the very point just made; besides, he adds, apart from Christ and the help of the Holy Spirit no one can keep God’s law, the Mosaic law being only workable by faith in Christ.

Theodoret takes the answer as a position which cannot be disputed and confirms it by the assertion that follows: it is one God, who is the God of all, one who is the Maker of all, nor is it possible that he should be careful for some and leave others uncared for, wherefore he extends his salvation to all that believe; by circumcision he means the Jews and by uncircumcision the Gentiles, and he next resolves the objection which might be raised. Of the last verse he says that of old both the law and the prophets prophesied of the things concerning the faith, and that in receiving the faith we therefore confirm the law; the Apostle then brings forward evidences of all this, and, while having it in his power to adduce a vast variety of testimonies from the prophets, prefers going at once to the very root of the Jews and demonstrates that the righteousness of the patriarch Abraham himself was that which is of faith.

debates: Whether the two prepositions differ: Clarke calls it fanciful to load them with different meanings and says the added article merely sharpens the second, and Barnes likewise finds no difference; Ellicott grants a slight one, instrument against means, with the anarthrous noun the more abstract; Robertson keeps it sharper, one marking source and the other intermediate agency; Calvin suspects irony, while reporting a serious version, that the Jews were born heirs of grace while to the Gentiles the covenant came from outside.

What law is established by faith: Calvin extends the defence to the whole law universally, ceremonies included, since these attain something solid only in their accomplishment in Christ; Barnes confines it to the moral law; Clarke divides it, the Mosaic rites established because Christ accomplished what they demanded and the moral law because faith works by love; Robertson adds that the Mosaic law is only workable by faith in Christ at all.

Whether the closing verse looks forward: Ellicott, against many commentators, treats it as an isolated assertion drawing on conclusions Paul had reached privately, the detailed proof being reserved for a much later place; Robertson and Theodoret both read it straight forward into the next chapter and the case of Abraham.
outliers: Barnes quotes verses of Watts on hating the sins that crucified the Lord, and calls this an advantage in moral influence which no cold abstract law ever has over the human mind.

Clarke closes the chapter with what a pious writer called the Catechism of Christian Righteousness, a series of questions and answers on the price paid, the blood, its application and its intended range, and with a warning against the Antinomian inference.
Calvin suggests that the change of preposition may be ironical, Paul offering the Jews the only difference they could possibly have between themselves and the Gentiles.
Robertson remarks that the Jews overlooked God’s being the God of the Gentiles then, and that some Christians do now.
